Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has


the minister's attention been drawn to a Canadian Press report appearing in today's Globe and Mail to the effect that Mr. Isaacs, trade minister for Jamaica, speaking in Kingston, Jamaica, yesterday referred to the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited, commonly known as NAFEL, as a dictatorial cartel which is doing great disservice to Newfoundland fishermen, and stated further that if Newfoundland fishermen want to continue selling codfish to Jamaica the Canadian government must smash this organization?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is giving the house information rather than asking for it. Can he not ask his question without so much statement of fact?
May I ask the minister whether in view of this statement he will tell the house what steps are being taken to preserve the Jamaican market for Newfoundland codfish?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo very kindly gave me notice of this question. I have seen the article. I do not think anybody here would use the words "dictatorial cartel" with respect to NAFEL, or that there is any inclination on the part of this government, again using the words of the article, to "smash" this organization. NAFEL is an organization for the marketing of fish which was set up under the government of Newfoundland prior to entering confederation, and that arrangement was continued for a period of five years after entering confederation. It has subsequently been renewed from year to year with notice that it would be subject to termination.
We have had a number of meetings connected with this particular problem. The Minister of Fisheries, the minister from Newfoundland and myself have conferred frequently on this matter together with the appropriate officials, and have been making a study of the entire problem of the marketing of fish from Newfoundland. We have had conferences with representatives of the industry from Newfoundland, and intend to have a further conference with them in the near future.
The market for Newfoundland fish in Jamaica and other parts of the West Indies and elsewhere is very important. We want to do everything in our power to preserve that market, and we are prepared to discuss with the importers of that fish the changes that perhaps are desirable in the methods of curing and packaging and things of that nature. The whole subject is under active consideration at the present time. We will

do everything possible to maintain the market in Jamaica for Newfoundland codfish.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister whether any decision has been reached as to the fate of NAFEL, whether it is going to be allowed to continue or is to be replaced by some other body?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, that is under consideration. As I stated earlier, there was no intention when Newfoundland entered confederation to have NAFEL continue as it had been set up in the past. At the end of the five year transitional period an extension was made from year to year with notification that that arrangement might be terminated at a time that would be suitable to all concerned. We are considering the matter now, but no decision has been reached at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to a question asked on Tuesday by the hon. member for Timiskaming, who inquired about the reported removal of the C.N.R. shops at Cochrane.
The management of the railway advise that the shop at Cochrane is a steam and not a diesel facility, and as such is not suitable for diesel maintenance work. In the dieseliza-tion program, which must be viewed against the broad background of system-wide operations, Senneterre, as the geographical centre of the railway division in that area, is the logical location as the diesel maintenance point.


Discussions have been held by supervisory officers with the appropriate labour union officers to explain fully the circumstances and to point out that it is necessary for the railway to keep up to date in technological and other forms of transport. Unless this is done the management feel it is inevitable that the railway would decline as a transportation agency and this, of course, would sharply reduce the employment opportunities for railway workers and accordingly would be against their long-term interests.
In the present transfer of work there, 17 employees are involved. Discussions have been held within the framework of the wage agreements, and when the discussions are concluded the employees will be in a position to declare their preference and take such options as are open to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday the hon. member for Vancouver East asked me a question with regard to the case of William Heikkila of San Francisco, as recorded on page 65 of Hansard. I should say by way of preface that the answer normally, I think, would be given by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, but as the incident took place while I had responsibility for that portfolio and as the question was directed to me, perhaps it is appropriate that I should give the reply.
The arrival of Mr. Heikkila in Canada was in accord with an informal reciprocal arrangement between Canada and the United States with regard to the entry into and transit through each of our respective countries of deportees from the other. This informal arrangement provides that the deportee shall be under escort provided by the deporting country at all times during such transit. It provides also for advance notification and proper record of entry and departure, all of which I am informed were complied with in this case.
The arrangement contemplates also that the country of transit is under no responsibility in making arrangements for the accommodation of the deportee during transit. In this case our immigration officers advised the United States escorting officers that our immigration building was not available for the detention of Heikkila during the period between his arrival and the departure of the plane on which his passage had been booked. Apparently the United States officers then made arrangements for his accommodation in a section of the Vancouver city jail. Such arrangements were made directly, and no immigration or other federal personnel were parties to them.
I might say that this is the first time the existence of the informal arrangement has come to my notice, and has led us to order a study of all its implications.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, May 15, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Green-Mr. Sevigny in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act. 1954, to increase from four hundred million dollars to seven hundred
National Housing Act
and fifty million dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act.

Mr. Chairman, at 10 o'clock last evening I had been mentioning some of the interesting information that had been given by the minister in introducing the resolution. Since that time, of course, I have been able to obtain yesterday's Hansard, so I do not have to rely on my notes which may or may not have been accurate. In his reference to increasing the 23 per cent to 27 per cent he made a most interesting disclosure. I read from page 117 of Hansard for May 15, 1958:
I believe it was increased from 23 per cent of a person's income to 27 per cent. The decision with regard to this proportion, of course, really rests with the lending institutions some of which I believe are still working on the 23 per cent basis.
What that means in essence, if I grasp correctly what the minister said, is that it is the private lending institutions who have control over the manner and to whom these public moneys will be lent. In fact the minister said that some of the institutions are still working on the 23 per cent basis. It will be most unfortunate if this house decides to loan public money to people to build homes, with which I am in complete agreement, and we then find that some outside financial interest has the final determination of the percentage bracket within which such a person is able to get that money.
In his usually humane and sincere manner the minister started off by showing an exceptionally fine attitude to the effect that the purpose of the government was to provide prospective home owners with the money to finance their own homes. I thought he was going to show a particularly fine socialist approach to home building, and that the government was going to go full speed ahead to provide this money and provide the means of owning their own homes to the people of this country. However, he dashed that thought to the ground pretty quickly when the so-called free enterprise thoughts in his mind came to the fore, for he said even though it is the policy of the government to help young Canadians to own homes and to do everything possible in that direction, nevertheless the government does not intend to become the main source of housing money but that the bulk of it would have to come from private lenders. He referred to the necessity of, I believe, finding $1,400 million and said that amount would have to be found somewhere for the purpose of home construction in this coming year.
We can only assume that the "somewhere" from whence this money will come is the same place from whence it has been coming

National Housing Act
in past years, that is to say from private lending institutions, financiers and banks. As the minister well knows from the past experience of both the Liberal government and his own government, and now from his own experience in administering his portfolio they will enter into the home building field to lend money only when they can profitably do so. If they find, as they have found in the past, that it is more profitable to put that money into other fields they will do so and will disregard the home building field.
The question therefore appears to be, how do we make it profitable for them? I believe it was in January, 1957, when the Liberal party was in office that the then minister of public works, Mr. Winters, discovered a way in which he could make it more profitable and lucrative for individual financial houses and banks to put their money into the home building field. That way was to raise the interest rate, and he accordingly increased it to 6 per cent. His remarks indicated that he anticipated that banks and other lending institutions would then be encouraged to make more loans under the act, which is precisely the same as the minister said yesterday except that he used different words. The former minister indicated that it was not possible or desirable to decrease the interest rate on home building loans to private citizens who wished to borrow money because, he said, if the government and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation decreased the interest rate it would then drive private lending institutions out of the field of home building loans; they would not lower their interest rate, which should be lowered, because they find it more lucrative to put their money into other fields.
The only possible inference we can draw from that statement is that the private lending institutions, banks and financial houses, are the ones who have control over the interest rate, and that applies on home building loans whether they come from public funds, as is provided in this resolution, or from private sources. If the government is going to be tied to the coat tails of financiers and lending institutions in establishing the interest rate, then when they decide not to put any more money into that field or when the federal government decides it cannot put any more money into that field, the only solution is to raise the interest rate from 6 per cent, which is the rate now existing, in order to draw in the required funds. All that will then happen is that it will increase the debt load on the people, the ordinary citizens who are buying or building homes, to an even greater degree than exists at present.
The minister wound up his statement yesterday with a flashing insight into the housing
[Mr. Howard.!
situation which had something to do with one or two of the comments made during the recent election. I believe he said that banks or other lending institutions have "caught the vision". I am quite sure they have caught the vision, Mr. Chairman, and it was not a vision which required the use of bifocals, either. It was the vision of high interest rates, the vision of the possibility of milking even more money from the citizens of this nation once they get into the position of being able to buy or own a home, and of creating the facilities for themselves and their families which we would all like to see them have.
Perhaps before going any further-this might be an anticipation based on a comment made by one of the hon. members of the Conservative party yesterday-and to allay their possible impatience, I should perhaps give our position on this resolution. This resolution is accepted by myself and this group but only with respect to the amount of money, not with respect to the manner in which that money will get into the hands of the people who want to build or buy homes, not with respect to the financial machinery as between this government, private lending institutions and banks.
I have in my hand some interesting figures as to just what this 6 per cent interest rate means, but before I quote them I would point out that, discounting the fact that the amount of money available under this section of the act has been increased, the attitude of this government is not one bit different from that of those who now sit to my left when they were in office. It is precisely the same. They said, "We do not want to compete with private enterprise. We are only going to step into the picture and use public funds when private enterprise, lending institutions and banks, decide they are not going to do it. We will then help them, will adjust the interest rate and make it more profitable for them." Even though, as the minister said, it is the policy of the present government to help young Canadians to own their own homes, I suggest that is only an incidental part of the attitude of this government. The main part is to the effect that they will help private lending institutions, they will assist them; and when they get into difficulty they will incidentally help the home owners.
With respect to the figures illustrating what this 6 per cent interest rate means I understand, and I am willing to be corrected if I am wrong, that the great number of persons taking loans under the National Housing Act take 25 year mortgages. There are some for less than that, but this 6 per cent interest rate, calculated as it is by Central Mortgage

and Housing Corporation or under the National Housing Act, means that a person pays back over a 25 year period an amount of $919.42 in interest for every $1,000 of original loan. By the first quarter of 1957 the average loan under the National Housing Act was $10,835, so taking the average and using the figure of additional interest of $919.42 per $1,000, we find that that person with a 25 year mortgage in addition to paying back the original loan of $10,800 odd pays an additional $9,951.83 in interest. He therefore pays almost the amount of his original loan in interest. It is a most disgusting drain on the purchasing power of our nation to force the people to pay money back at these usurious rates in order to buy homes.
There is one way in which we could combat these high interest rates. That is for the government to follow through with its original intention as expressed by the minister, when he said the policy was to help young Canadians to own their own homes. He should do this in a more forceful manner, in a direct manner and as a principal part of government policy instead of as an incidental part of this home building program, and the way to do that would be to use the facilities of government we have today in order to lend people their own money at interest rates comparable to what it costs to administer and provide the loans.
All we are asking is the application of the principles of credit unionism to the operation of our home building program in Canada, and for the establishment of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as a Canadian-owned or citizen-owned credit union lending people back their own money at interest rates which are not so high or so usurious as those charged by financial institutions and banks.
Another problem is raised by the number of people who require subsidization before they can possibly own or rent housing accommodation of any kind, people such as old age pensioners and those living on low fixed incomes. The only solution to this problem, to my way of thinking, is to subsidize the cost of providing these facilities to a greater extent than we do at the moment.
I do not wish to refer to the previous administration more than is necessary, but I think I must do so in this case because the former government was in office at the time a great deal of work was done under the National Housing Act, and a considerable number of homes and apartments were built while it was in office. The results of that program, generally, were most disgraceful not only to the government and to citizens
National Housing Act
who could not afford to buy homes, but to the nation as a whole. I do not know how much the figures have been changed since the 1951 census, but I should like to mention one or two of the latest statistics available in order to indicate something of the situation which then existed. It was estimated that in 1951 there were 450,000 homes which needed repair or remodelling and that 175,000 of these were overcrowded. Incidentally, that figure of 175,000 applies only to cities with populations of 30,000 or more and disregards all the people who do not have houses in cities with populations of 30,000 or more. Twenty-five per cent of the homes had no running water; 35 per cent had no indoor facilities, and 43 per cent had no baths or showers. Some hon. members have talked about vacuum cleaners, telephones and so on, but these are extra items.
If the government persists in its present attitude, tying itself to the coat tails of financial institutions with respect to how much money it will put into the housing field and juggling the interest rate at the desire and whim of the banks and other lending institutions, then its approach to this problem is no better than the approach of the government it superseded with the exception, as I said before, that the amount of money available has been increased. The general approach is no different.
I know many places in my own riding of Skeena-and I have just visited them- which are not included in the 1951 census because they form parts of communities which have a population of less than 30,000.
I may add that there is no community in the riding of Skeena which has 30,000 people living in it, and accordingly we are not considered in this particular part of the 1951 census. But I know many homes in Skeena which need repair. People have not sufficient money to repair them, and they cannot get it. They cannot get loans under the National Housing Act, even under its present provisions, except through a chartered bank, because private mortgage companies, trust companies and other institutions which lend money for home building in the province of British Columbia will not step outside the boundaries of the city of Vancouver with the exception, perhaps, of those places which they have entered in the southern interior. They will not go into northern British Columbia because they find it is not worth their while to invest their money in that part of the province. They find they can invest their money more profitably in Vancouver and other large urban areas than they could in other portions of the country which, nevertheless, have greater needs than have the

National Housing Act
large urban areas with regard to repairing homes, overcoming overcrowding and matters of that nature.
Maybe my remarks have been somewhat critical; nevertheless I believe they have been constructive. If they have been critical it is because we in this group have always taken a great deal of interest in housing, and because we have had some sorry experiences in connection with the operations of C.M.H.C. in the past. I am sure the minister is familiar with the criticisms which were raised by home owners in Kitimat, and I understand his department is dealing with this matter now if it has not done so already.
Again, if my comments have sounded critical it is because we have a keen desire to operate the machinery and finances of government for the sole purpose of assisting the people of Canada and for the putting into effect of what the minister claims to be the policy of this government, namely to provide the citizens of this nation with facilities to own their own homes.
Before I close I should like to leave one question with the minister. As recorded on page 116 of Hansard he said:
We made an agreement with the lending institutions of Canada, including the banks, that they would act as our agents in the placing of these loans for what we considered was a reasonable fee.
It may well be that the minister's interpretation of what is a reasonable fee differs from my own, and I should like to discover whether or not this is so.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my first remarks today should be words of congratulations to you on your election to the important post you now occupy. I am sure you will discharge your responsibilities in a manner that befits the traditions of this house.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this measure for several reasons. For many years I have had a strong interest in the general subject of housing and a keen awareness of its importance to our people. I recall that my first remarks in this parliament back in 1949 were directed to the subject of housing.
May I at once refer in a complimentary way to the splendid achievements in this field, and in particular to the job done by the government through its agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Those of us who have taken an interest in this subject are well aware of the various changes and improvements in the national housing legislation under Liberal administration down through the years to cope with changing conditions and circumstances. While this legislation did not always meet with the full approval of all of us I think all will agree that it has made

a tremendous contribution toward filling a very vital need in our country. As practical proof I need only remind you of the hundreds of thousands of homes that have been completed as a result of this national housing legislation.
We welcome this measure not only because of the great need that exists for improved housing in this country, we welcome it especially in view of the confusion which I believe has been created in the housing industry in these past several months. There seems to be a lack of clear-cut government policy on housing. When I questioned the minister yesterday I was hoping for some information that would indicate government policy. Instead I received a short explanation of the "vision". In respect to the matter I raise I suggest the only reason more money is being put into housing-if in fact more will be put in-is because of a slackening in the demand for money in more attractive fields rather than as a result of any government policy or action. I was hoping to have some comment on that yesterday; yet the minister, I suppose understandably, wants to give credit to the "vision".
There apparently is only passing recognition on the part of the government of the fact that the houses now being built are beyond the reach of the families who need them most. I noticed that the minister in his remarks made no reference to the increase in the price of lots, which have increased during the last few years by over 300 per cent as substantiated by government figures.
The minister says on the one hand that the government does not intend to supply mortgage funds, that the leading institutions are fulfilling this need to a greater degree; yet in this legislation the government is asking for more public funds than ever before. It would seem to me that the people of this country expect a clearer statement of government policy with respect to housing.
One of the prime requisites of a buoyant economy is confidence in government, but I believe the present government's policy leaves much to be desired in the field of housing. I do not wish to be unduly critical, but let us look at the facts. It is common knowledge that for the past several months housing has required substantially more financial assistance than was given by the government. Proof of this fact can be provided by the way available money was gobbled up by the industry. In the midst of this the minister, speaking to a convention of the building industry, reminded his audience that they should not look to the federal government to supply mortgage funds, and he

reiterated that view yesterday. This statement was made during the worst period of unemployment this country has experienced since the thirties.
Those of us interested in housing were curious to know what action the government did propose. If more money was not forthcoming, what was being done? What was going to be done to encourage the lending institutions to provide more funds? We looked for legislation at the last session, but none was forthcoming, nor apparently is any foreshadowed in the throne speech.
Then we moved along to early March and we had the comments of the Prime Minister on the subject of mortgage funds for housing. The Prime Minister's statement, of course, came in the midst of an election campaign, when I understand he was confronted by newspapermen who reminded him that housing money had been exhausted. He immediately replied that more funds would be provided, yet our construction industry has lost at least two months in a valuable building period. Here again is proof of the lack of government planning, to have this important segment of our economy held up as it has been for these past several weeks.
In my home city of North Bay I know from actual representations that have been made to me that several people are experiencing delays in their construction because of the lack of government funds for house building. I believe this delay was entirely unnecessary and is the direct result of the lack of government planning and foresight, or perhaps I should add "vision". If the government really believes that this construction will assist in relieving the unemployment situation why was sufficient money not provided months ago to save the needless suffering associated with unemployment?
Desirable though construction of new housing may be, it is not a cure-all for our present economic problems, which can be cured only by putting more spending money into the hands of our people by immediate tax reductions with special emphasis on tax relief in the lower income brackets.
This, Mr. Chairman, leads me to another aspect in the matter of housing. As always, the greatest need for assistance in housing remains with those in the moderate and lower income brackets. Surely this fact is apparent to all. Surely the people of Canada have a right to expect this government with its huge majority to do something about it. After all, conditions change and with these changes the needs of our society change. It will scarcely be enough for this government to get out the old "business as usual" sign in these fields in which they promised bold and courageous action if ever elected.
National Housing Act
The National Housing Act, introduced and improved upon over the years by the Liberal government, has served Canada well but it needs changes to meet the new conditions of 1958. I believe income requirements under the act should be altered, thereby making National Housing Act mortgages available to more Canadians. May I also suggest that National Housing Act valuation procedures be brought up to date to take account of the real values of houses in 1958. These and other measures should be taken to make it easier for our people to acquire new homes with lower down payments.
Surely there is room for imaginative action, for a study of the varied needs of our people in the field of housing. Housing design in this country seems to be based on the assumption that all families are the same size. It would appear that all houses are built to accommodate the husband and wife of a family and two or three children. Needless to say, much accommodation is wasted because we have failed to keep pace with this aspect of the needs of our people. Think for a moment of the accommodation needed for couples without a family. Think of the accommodation required by single people. Think of the need for smaller units for our elderly citizens. Yet every house that is constructed is built on the popular assumption that it will be occupied by this standard size family of four or five that I mentioned earlier. I would like to go into this matter in more detail, and perhaps I will have an opportunity to do so at a later date as I do not wish to unduly delay the passage of the measure now before us.
Another matter that deserves the immediate attention of the government is the rate of interest charged. I believe it is grossly unfair to have our low income wage earners competing with high salaried executives for the same loans at the same rate of interest. Further, I think the time has come when people in the lower income brackets should not have to compete with industry for mortgage funds. Surely it is the people in the moderate and lower income brackets who are in need of protection in this regard, and I believe the time has arrived when consideration should be given to lowering the rate of interest charged borrowers whose yearly income does not exceed $4,000. I consider it unfair that the government should make a profit by borrowing money from the Canadian people at rates ranging from 2J per cent to 3J per cent and forcing our lower income borrowers to pay 6 per cent. This is the time when a new look should be taken at this matter.
I believe further that consideration should be given to a longer period of amortization

National Housing Act
on loans made to the average and lower income borrowers. These are the people our legislation is intended to assist. That was the spirit of the legislation when it was introduced. However, increased costs and other circumstances have intervened, so I believe a thorough study of this aspect of the legislation should be made at the earliest opportunity.
The discussion of this measure also gives me the opportunity to remind the government of a matter I raised in the house last year, namely the problem experienced by many communities across Canada of under 50,000 population. Here we find the continual siphoning off of investment money to the large metropolitan areas. It is not my intention to go into this matter in any detail at this time, but I think all hon. members are well aware of this problem and are keenly aware of its seriousness and its detrimental effect on the development of our smaller cities across the country. I am sure hon. members are well aware of the attitude of many of our lending institutions which do business in every community in Canada yet refuse to lend funds in the majority of these same communities. I think, too, it is reasonable to expect that these companies will become even more selective in their lending practices in periods of economic recession such as we are experiencing at the present time.
I recognize the right and the responsibility of these lending institutions to invest their customers' funds to the best possible advantage, and I am not suggesting government interference or compulsion. However, I do suggest that there be discussions along these lines between the government and the lending institutions in regard to the sort of practice I have referred to, which I believe does retard the normal growth and development of large sections of this country. Too many times we see these lending institutions doing a substantial volume of business in our communities yet refusing to lend a dollar in these same areas where they are doing business.
In the field of housing this has meant one of two things; either the government must come to the rescue and supply the local needs, as they have been doing over the years, or our people are driven to rely on the mercy of loan sharks who extract exorbitant rates of interest and bonuses. Here again the people in the moderate and lower income brackets are more seriously affected.
Further, I believe the government should give encouragement to developing, in cooperation with the provinces and the municipalities, more serviced land. Surely no

greater contribution could be made to the people in the medium and lower income brackets than to make available to them for house building purposes as soon as possible reasonably priced and adequately serviced building lots.
I would like to refer to yet another aspect that has crept into our present-day situation. I have in mind the greatest single contributing factor to the unreasonably high prices of our so-called low-priced homes. I am referring to the cost of land, which is the real issue today. Too many times we have seen ordinary farm land turned into a housing development, with resultant overnight increases in land values running higher than 1,000 per cent. Please do not misunderstand me. I am not against regular profits, but I am against the use of public funds in the promotion of some of these high priced and high pressure subdivision developments which we have seen emerge across this country in the last few years. The government should take whatever action is necessary to ensure that public money is not used for this purpose in the future. The money we are discussing today should go into housing and not into the purses of unscrupulous land developers.
While supporting this legislation, I do urge the government to give more attention to the real needs that exist in providing better housing for our Canadian people. I believe there is a great opportunity for this new government to provide leadership in this important field.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to offer you my most sincere congratulations on your election to the post of Deputy Speaker of this house. We know, of course, that you will acquit yourself worthily of this task, even though it might not always be a pleasant one.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to thank the electors of the constituency of St. Ann who have chosen me for a second time to be their spokesman in this house. This is, for me, an honourable task, one which I shall never fail to accomplish with pleasure whenever I have the opportunity of defending their rights in this house.
The question of housing, of slum clearance and of low cost housing is a matter of the very highest importance as far as I am concerned, representing as I do one of the oldest constituencies of the city of Montreal where about 70 per cent of homes lack a bathtub or shower or any number of those other facilities which are necessary in this day and age.

That is why I want to put forward at this time the views of the electors of St. Ann with regards to the National Housing Act so that all members of this house will understand the need of making it easier for people to take advantage of this act, by pointing out the evils attendant upon the existence of slums and suggesting the improvements that should be brought to the act. In any number of our streets there are houses whose main entrance opens on a back yard. In many cases people who live on the second or third floor of houses without a street door get into their dwelling by climbing flights of stairs which are little more than fire traps for these good workers and heads of households who, as often as not, cannot count all the members of their family on the fingers of their two hands. Those backstairs are their only exit and I wonder what protection those honest citizens have against fire and what facilities can be found in those houses. What encouragement is there for our youth? As I said in the last parliament, it is our duty to ensure comfort to our future generation, which is our greatest wealth.
A study committee of slum clearance in Montreal, which analysed the problem, marked out four slum areas in my constituency. That is why I fight and will continue to fight for the disappearance of those substandard houses, so that they may be replaced by low cost houses. What is the good of developing the city to the north, the east and the west and letting it go to pot in the south? That is why the provisions of the NHA must be more accessible and acceptable to the city.
The Minister of Public Works told us last night that it was the desire of the government that every Canadian should have his own home. I fully support also the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier when he said that we, on this side of the house, were happy to see the NHA fund increased by $350 million to reach a reach a maximum of $750 million.
However, the minister should not imagine that this addition will make the act perfect in every respect. Many finishing touches are lacking regarding the interest rate, which is too high, as well as the down payment and, moreover, with regard to the amortization period which should be extended.
However, for the moment, Mr. Chairman, I shall merely discuss the efficiency of the NHA with regard to slum clearance and low rental housing.
National Housing Act
During last session, when the Minister of Public Works had asked the house to vote some $150 million and approve a few minor improvements to the NHA, I had made a few suggestions which, in my humble opinion, would have made the legislation more attractive for cities and townships which are plagued with slums.
I do not wonder that the hon. minister has not agreed to introduce into the act the suggestions I had made during this discussion; however, I shall do so again today, and as long as I am a member of parliament, I will rise to submit to the government the changes I still think essential in this legislation.
I said at the last session, more precisely on December 18, 1957, when Bill 238, that is the National Housing Act, was before the house, that I could see no reason why the contribution of the federal government should be 75 per cent of the cost of construction of family units and only 50 per cent of the cost of expropriation of slums.
The raising to 75 per cent of the federal contribution to slum clearance would be justified. It would encourage many municipalities to clear up their slums and substandard housing.
I had also asked the extension of the credit facilities provided for in section 5 of the NHA for the implementation of paragraph (h) of section 33 dealing with studies concerning slum clearance in co-operation with provinces and municipalities. There is no reason why the federal government should not pay at least 75 per cent of the cost of such studies.
In the city of Montreal, the metropolis of Canada, there are many slum areas which are bound to be eliminated. At the present time one section is being cleared and, under the NHA, low priced sanitary housing units will be built there.
Thus, those blighted areas will be replaced by modern buildings inhabited by happy families. At a modest rental, compatible with the low income of poor families, those people will be provided with living quarters having windows in every room, to let the sun in, and equipped with all sanitary and modern conveniences.
I cannot understand, Mr. Chairman, why the Minister of Public Works should ask the house to increase by $350 million the sum available under the NHA, without improving

National Housing Act
that legislation and without making any change to encourage cities and municipalities to take advantage of that measure to improve the living conditions of some of their citizens who are housed in slums, a situation which should not be tolerated in a rich and young country such as Canada.
In support of what I have just said, Mr. Chairman, I have clipped an article entitled:
Necessary restoration in Montreal
which appeared in yesterdays' edition of La Presse. It is about a lecture given in Montreal by a member of the government who is well acquainted with the slum question, I mean the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Campeau), a former director of town planning for the city of Montreal, a man who had all the necessary opportunity to study the slum situation in Montreal.
Here is what the paper reports:
... at a meeting held in the parish hall of St. Nicholas of Ahuntsic, in connection with an embellishment campaign organized by the Montreal Property Owners' League, Mr. Campeau stated that we must tackle the slum problem, this real urban cancer . . .
It is indeed a cancer which, in cities like Montreal, has a tendency to spread. That is why, Mr. Chairman, I asked last year and am still asking today and shall go on pressing for the insertion of certain provisions in the NHA, in order that it may be made more readily available to municipalities, so that cities will not have to spend huge sums of money.
According to Mr. Campeau, speaking at the same conference last night, there are:
. . . about 2,000 housing units in Montreal which were built before 1870.
I do not know enough about it to verify this statement, but I do know that Mr. Campeau, who was director of the town planning service for the city of Montreal, knows what he is talking about. This means that those
2.000	housing units built before 1870 should have been demolished long ago.
Mr. Campeau also said:
At least 25,000 housing units are substandard, and
10.000	are slums.
Besides the 2,000 units built before 1870, there are, according to Mr. Campeau, 10,000 in the slum category.
It can therefore be considered that about 25,000 housing units should be torn down.
That is why I urge, as I said a moment ago, and shall keep on urging that this legislation be improved.

Now, I have a question I wish to ask of the minister. I shall ask it first in French, and then in English, because I want to make sure that the minister will understand it and give me a satisfactory answer. Is the hon. minister aware that the Department of National Revenue would like to acquire for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the site expropriated by the city of Montreal to carry out jointly with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the low rental housing project called "Les habitations Jeanne Mance"? If so, does the Department of Public Works intend to cancel the contracts entered into with the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec in connection with the said project?

Mr. Chairman, I am entirely in accord with the resolution, which is now before the committee. I agree that the provision of the funds in question would be of great advantage to the citizens of Canada. I feel obliged to concur in one aspect of the matter which has been raised by members who have spoken previously. I refer to the fact that the lending institutions, as well as

National Housing Act
Central Mortgage and Housing, are reluctant to go into the smaller centres to make housing loans. I am not speaking only of the small villages, but I am speaking of the towns and smaller cities. We can understand their reluctance because, in the first place, the facilities for making loans and checking on building progress are definitely limited in these areas. On the other hand the intention in providing these funds is to enable all the people in the country to build homes.
It has been my experience that when a loan is provided in a small community-I think this has been the experience of many hon. members-the processing is considerably slower and the standards of living in smaller centres are different from those in such large cities as Vancouver, Toronto and Ottawa. As a result the lending institutions just do not want to be bothered with these small loans.
That is all I wanted to say on the subject, because I am definitely in favour of the resolution and the provision of the money. However, I would ask the minister to make an effort to encourage the lending institutions to put out these loans in some of the smaller centres so that all the people will benefit equally.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, once again this morning I should like to thank hon. members who have been making these suggestions. Perhaps I could deal right away with some of the points that have been mentioned. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, as well as the hon. member for Nipissing, mentioned the need for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to take a greater interest in the smaller centres in Canada. I referred to that situation last evening, and I should like to assure those hon. members and other members of the house that I am very much interested in every effort being made to provide loans in the smaller centres. We will have a very careful look to see what can be done to improve this situation.
Then the hon. member for Skeena referred to Kitimat. There has been some trouble there with regard to the quality of the houses that were built, the money for which had been provided by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This crown company has no direct responsibility for the quality of the houses. We do, however, inspect them and as a result of that fact the owners do get the impression-I think honestly held-that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is guaranteeing the workmanship of the homes. The corporation does do its best to see that builders construct proper homes but in some cases, and Kitimat is a good example, some homes have not been properly built.

When I learned of this situation I happened, as a matter of fact, to be visiting Kitimat on political business-rather unsuccessfully, I might add-and I promised to have the executive assistant to the president go to Kitimat and look into the whole situation and endeavour to work out some solution. This has now been done, and I am hoping that as a result of his visit these people who have suffered will have at least some of their grievances removed.
Then the hon. member asked me for the rate paid to the lending institutions for handling the loans under the small home loans plan. Under the agency agreement between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the approved lender the latter receives for making and advancing a loan a fee of $100 for each loan made in respect of a house other than to a builder, and $90 for each loan made in respect of a house to a builder. Smaller amounts are paid in respect to multiple family dwellings. A fee of one-half of 1 per cent per annum on the principal outstanding on ownership loans and one-quarter of 1 per cent in respect of loans for rental housing is also paid to the approved lender for administering the loan.
Normally the non-recurring cost to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for each application to place as an ordinary insured loan is 1 per cent of the amount of the loan after taking into account the application fee paid by the borrower. The agency fees involve approximately an additional 1 per cent. On this basis, the total agency loan commitments of $260 million, which is the amount that has been loaned out to date, would involve processing costs to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation of approximately $2.6 million and fees to lenders representing a further $2.6 million. As the principal of the loans is a public fund the interest yield, of course, accrues to the government to offset these costs.
The hon. member for Nipissing thought the construction industry had lost too much time this spring because of money having run out. That statement was not accurate because some of the homes for which loans had been made under the small home loans plan had not been put under construction at the time. In other words there were many starts made during these intervening weeks when we have been short of money; and, as I pointed out last night, the lending institutions and the banks have taken on about 75 per cent of the applications which had come into Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but which had not yet been dealt with. The building figures still show that there has been no slump at all this year; building is going on at a very rapid pace, more rapidly than ever

before in Canada's history; and of course one of our main objectives is to avoid any such slump.
The hon. member for St. Ann really dragged in the Department of Public Works in connection with the Jeanne Mance development plan in Montreal. The Department of Public Works is not in charge of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This crown company merely reports through the Minister of Public Works and the president of the corporation has the status of deputy minister, so I am quite sure that if the Department of Public Works or the Department of National Revenue tried to stage a raid on a plan of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that raid would not be very successful, and we will not allow the Department of National Revenue to ruin the Jeanne Mance plan. I believe there is now some difficulty in connection with that plan, which has been brought about by a failure to agree at the municipal level, but has nothing whatever to do with the federal government.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver East, a very old friend of mine, mentioned the exorbitant rate of interest charged on second mortgages.
Also on first mortgages.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not understand why there should be an exorbitant rate of that kind on a first mortgage in Vancouver if there is not something wrong with the proposal. I quite agree that such rates are charged on second mortgages, and there had been a great deal of that type of business going on before this small home loans plan was initiated. I am, however, confident that the plan has done a good deal to wipe out this sort of exorbitant charge, and in Vancouver under the plan there has been over $7 million loaned for 782 units, which is quite a lot of building in a matter of eight months.
The aim of the government has been and will be to extend these benefits just as widely as possible to people of modest income in this country. We are not a bit interested in the people who are well able to finance their own homes. Mind you, we are glad to see them build, but our aim is to help the Canadian with the small income. We will be trying throughout to extend these benefits further and further down the line to the lower income groups.
One big difficulty we face is that housing is getting more and more expensive. Moreover, as several hon. members have said, the land costs more. I heartily agree that there has been a tremendous increase in the cost of land. This is one of the very difficult problems which face us, and it is a problem
National Housing Act
which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation cannot solve alone. It may be that with the cities of Canada growing as they are we just have to expect that land is going tn remain at a high price. But, as I say, this is a very serious problem and one which is giving us a great deal of worry.
All the suggestions which have been made will be given consideration and we will be very glad, also, to receive representations at any time even if they are not made here in the house. We are trying to help the Canadian people to get homes, or to help them get apartments at reasonable rates if they do not want homes, and government policy will be designed with those objectives always in mind.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few brief observations which I would like to make on this resolution. This proposed legislation will make available an extra $350 million of federal funds for housing. In December of last year, during the last session, we made available $150 million in addition to the $250 million which had been provided by the late administration prior to the election of June 10. With the passage of this legislation, the total amount of federal funds available for housing will have reached the unprecedented figure of three-quarters of a billion dollars.

Yes, I understand that. Like other hon. members on the opposition side of the house I support this legislation, because I realize it is being put through as part of an emergency program in an effort to alleviate the unemployment situation and also to help counteract the serious down turn in our economy which Canada is experiencing at the present time. But since these funds are the taxpayers' own money, coming from the consolidated revenue fund, and since they are being provided for the purpose I have just mentioned, there is all the more reason to see to it that they are distributed in such a way as to provide equal benefit to all the provinces of Canada.
The unemployment situation and economic conditions in Newfoundland are the worst since the hungry thirties-worse, probably,, than any other province in Canada-yet though our problem is the greatest in Canada, Newfoundland will receive the least benefit of all from these funds. The minister has told us that the $400 million previously provided is practically exhausted. I would ask him, if figures are available, to place them on record so as to show how that sum of $400 million has been distributed among

National Housing Act
the various provinces. I am sure the figures will show that an unduly large share, proportionately, has gone to the wealthy provinces of Ontario and British Columbia and an unduly small proportion to the poorer maritime provinces, with Newfoundland receiving the smallest share of all.
This must always be the case as long as these funds are distributed on the basis of average income, because in the maritimes in general and particularly in Newfoundland we have proportionately poorer people whose average incomes are too low to enable them to benefit from this legislation under present regulations. An income basis may be a very convenient basis upon which to distribute these funds, but it is not altogether a fair basis because in most cases people in low income brackets have the largest families and consequently need bigger houses than people in the higher income brackets. Since the need for increased employment and improved economic conditions is equally great in all provinces, some more equitable basis of distribution should be found in order to enable all provinces to benefit equally from funds which are made available from the federal treasury.
When one considers the increasing demand for federal funds and the large sum of $750 million which this legislation will make available, one cannot help wondering whether our free enterprise system is facing up to its responsibilities in providing housing for our citizens. With the construction industry becoming more and more dependent on federal funds for housing, one wonders also how the federal government will ever be able to retrace its steps in this field. One thing is certain; the availability of federal funds for housing has greatly inflated the cost of housing and especially land values. Thus in solving, or in attempting to solve, one problem we are creating another.
In order to minimize these disadvantages, these detrimental effects, I believe federal funds should be used mainly for the provision of low cost housing for people whose income is below the national average. This would include low cost homes with no down payment and low rental houses for people who cannot afford to own homes at all. I am particularly interested in low cost homes for fishermen who do not require houses built to standard specifications, and I should be grateful if the minister would see what progress is being made in this respect.
Another way to offset the inflationary effects of federal funds for housing would be the encouragement of co-operative housing schemes. I have had some personal experience in this field, because I helped to organize

a veterans' co-operative group following the second world war. The members of this group were able to build homes at little more than half the contractor's price. I know that when properly organized a co-operative housing plan can be highly successful, and I urge the government to give every possible encouragement to this form of housing activity.

Mr. Chairman, three hon. members including my good friend the hon. member for Fort William have alluded to the difficulties encountered by small towns in obtaining loans through the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The minister has given us an assurance that he is going to do something about it, but I wondered if I gave a few examples of the difficulties that are experienced in my constituency it would assist him to see that it will take something definite and concrete to remedy the situation, and not just a general assurance on his part that the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have the best of intentions. I have discovered in the lakehead area that they have excellent intentions indeed and know the situation very well, but while they have not told me this I believe it is obvious that they are hamstrung by sheer economic difficulties.
When you are building housing there are a number of determining factors, including the going wage rates in the area for carpenters and other construction workers. It happens that in our constituency, which is roughly 600 by 300 miles in size, there is a scattering of small towns. Throughout these communities union contracts prevail pretty generally, so that carpenters' rates are well over $2 an hour. At the same time these communities are distant from any central point such as Port Arthur, which is tucked in the southwest corner and which would provide them with materials and other supplies necessary for house construction. I am thinking of plumbing supplies, concrete blocks and that sort of thing. In other words the main distribution point for our particular area is not in a good location to ship builders' supplies, let us say, to a high income community such as Hornepayne, which is roughly 340 miles from Port Arthur. At the present time Hornepayne does not have a single house provided under the National Housing Act, despite the fact that it is perhaps the highest income community in my whole constituency because it is a busy railway divisional point.
The situation is further aggravated in my constituency by the fact that we have in this isolated area a number of communities that have exceptionally good housing. These are what might be called company towns. For

example there is splendid housing at Mani-towadge in the centre of the constituency, which has been supported by the Geco mine. We also have Terrace Bay and Marathon, which are pulp and paper towns. Very enlightened company management influenced by the United States example have gone ahead and given the people a standard of housing that is superior to the standard obtaining in the city of Port Arthur. So we have existing in juxtaposition communities such as Gerald-ton, Beardmore and Longlac that have a very low standard of housing. As a matter of fact, I obtained figures which indicate that in the first six months of last year only four homes were built under the National Housing Act outside the city of Port Arthur.
The officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have been making serious efforts to extend direct lending in these communities beyond the lakehead, but so far they have not been too successful. The answer, as I see it, is that you cannot economically build a house in these distant communities that people can afford to pay for unless there is some form of subsidy- and let us not be ashamed of the word "subsidy"-that will give the people in these distant communities a chance to obtain satisfactory housing. In addition I feel there must be some change in the requirement regulations so that as far as actual land assembly is concerned there will be some provision for waiving certain of these requirements so that people in distant towns and municipalities that do not have services and facilities available can do something about it. This would be applicable particularly in communities such as Hornepayne.
The Nakina situation is going to be greatly aggravated this year because the Kimberly-Clark Pulp and Paper Company is going to construct not far distant from the town what will be in effect a model community. I feel very strongly that Nakina itself should have Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials in there doing something to improve housing within that community. At the present time the break-even point for a contractor under Central Mortgage and Housing terms in communities distant from supply centres, as is the case in Nakina, is pretty poor.
I could be mistaken in my interpretation of the difficulty, but the views I have expressed are those I hold as the result of talking to municipal officers in the constituency and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials in Fort William, whom I have found to be exemplary. I could not speak in higher terms of their interest and general devotion to their job.
National Housing Act
There is one further point in this connection. If you do present some form of inducement to build in the smaller and more distant towns, whether it is an advantage attached to the interest rate, an easing of the regulations or some form of encouragement to the municipalities, one final thing needs to be done and done much more. I am referring to the form of publicity that takes place in those communities. The kind of publicity that is most effective is that of having a representative of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation visit a centre with adequate time to acquaint the people in that community with what is available to them under the act. I suggest to the minister that it is impossible for the officials located in Fort William to travel east and west and really do a job in these communities in terms of selling the people on taking advantage of what is available under the act, in view of the size of the present staff. I would ask him to consider putting more men on who could launch a campaign of acquainting the people in the small communities with the minister's idea of modest homes. I would remind the minister that only 17 per cent of the loans made last year under the act were obtained by people living in communities of 5,000 population. This should be a spur and incentive to increased activity in this field.
Mr. Chairman, as there are one or two other matters I wish to speak about may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, before lunch I had completed the argument that I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with some steps that could be taken by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to improve the loans situation in the small communities. The other two things that I want to touch on briefly relate to the use of National Housing Act funds for dormitories and residences at universities. This matter was brought up by Mr. Brown, the then member for Essex West in the last house, and I know from reading the records of the university conference that it was an idea that was very close to the heart of the present Speaker of this house. I just hope that in the general consideration that the minister will be giving to this act he will find time to consider it again and try to implement

National Housing Act
this important means of helping our universities and colleges to go ahead with residence buildings through the use of National Housing Act funds. I know that at the present time [DOT]Canada Council funds are being used for this purpose on a sort of direct grant basis. I think right across the country the principle could be established in a general way and the funds used more in the form of general aid rather than the specific help that some colleges manage to get from the Canada Council.
The third point that I want to touch on deals with the question of a moratorium in connection with foreclosures. When he spoke in Windsor last November I understand the minister made the statement that there would be no foreclosures in any situation where a person was unemployed and unable to keep up with his payments; at least that is the record that I was able to find. We have one *community in our area at the present time that has suffered an economic downturn after a great deal of housing was constructed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I point out to the hon. member that that reference was to *evictions.

Thank you, I stand corrected. I would like to suggest that an official statement on the way in which a moratorium on foreclosures could be developed, if made, would give a great deal of heart to certain communities where there has been an economic downturn. I think of mining communities such as Atikokan where the miners have *entered into the whole spirit of the community. They have settled down there and bought houses. They have been laid off. Other mines, for example, in the uranium ureas have been established and the officials have come into Atikokan and induced the miners to move. In some instances miners who have moved have had to sell out at a tremendous disadvantage. In other instances, they have stayed in Atikokan without work, hoping to be taken back. If they knew that they were protected by some regulation of the minister through the National Housing Act it would do a great deal for the confidence of the people in those communities. In certain instances where the people are out of work on a sort of temporary basis, if there could be some special consideration given by *way of a waiving of interest for a period it would be of great assistance to those people.
This concludes the remarks I wanted to make on this bill, except to congratulate the minister on bringing it in and also for giving *us the opportunity to bask in the general beneficence that he displays when he brings ihis bills into the house.

Mr. Chairman, if I rise to say a few words on the resolution stage of the bill I wish to say that it is not my intention to oppose the resolution. I realize and I fully understand that further sources of money are required if the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to carry out its program, but I feel it is our duty as members of the opposition to offer some constructive suggestions which could result in a better and more practical application of the act.
Last year when a similar bill was introduced in the house I mentioned that even with the amendments which were then included in the measure it would not reach the objective that the bill had in mind so far as the Atlantic provinces were concerned. I recall also that when the Minister of Public Works introduced his bill, or rather when he made the announcement to the press before introducing the bill late in November of last year, made a statement to the effect that an additional $150 million would be made available for low-cost housing mortgages and that the changes to the act and regulations were being introduced partly to help maritime residents to take advantage of the scheme. I recall also that when speaking on the second reading of the bill I welcomed the additional amount which was then added to the fund and made available under the act as well as the provisions for reduced or lower down payments.
I well remember saying at the time that the changes would be of limited or of very little effect so far as the Atlantic provinces were concerned. In fact from April 1 to November 30 of last year only 240 loans had been approved by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the Atlantic provinces for a total amount of less than $2,225,000. I recall also stating at the time that during the same period loans for a similar amount were made in the city of Windsor alone.
Furthermore, during the debate I brought to the attention of the minister the brief which was submitted in September of last year to the minister, the government and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation by the national retail lumbermen's council. The minister assured me at the time that the recommendations in the brief were under serious study and consideration by officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I have the feeling, however, that even at this late date very few if any of the national retail lumbermen's council recommendations have been accepted or included in the standards and requirements of the National Housing Act.

Before this present resolution is adopted could the minister inform this committee as to the number of loans approved in the Atlantic provinces from January 1 of this year to, say, March 31 or even to April 30, if the figures are available; also the total amount involved to cover such loans.
Have the Atlantic provinces taken full advantage of this scheme which, according to the minister's own words, was further implemented when the government realized that there was a dark cloud of unemployment coming up over the horizon last fall. We are prepared to admit that there was a dark cloud of unemployment and that cloud has been hanging over the Atlantic provinces for at least the last seven or eight months.
Again, I cannot agree with the minister's statement to the effect that the people of the Atlantic provinces were directly to be blamed for not taking full advantage of the money made available to them for the construction of new houses by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Is it not simply because they cannot meet the high standards and requirements of the act? Is it not also because they cannot meet a gross debt service ratio of up to 27 per cent? We have in the Atlantic provinces a large number of wage earners whose income does not exceed $45 to $60 a week. They are the people who are in urgent need of new homes and they are the people who should and could be helped by the act if proper regulations were included in it.
It is mainly by a longer amortization period for the repayment of loans and by lower interest rates that housing can be provided for people in the lower income brackets. It may be that the government can be commended for having taken a step in the right direction by asking parliament to provide additional funds to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but the minister will agree that this does not go far enough and is not altogether practical. The changes made last year may have helped to some extent but we must admit that by increasing the gross debt ratio of the low income bracket wage earner from 23 per cent to 27 per cent we are not rendering a service to the person involved.
For example, the mortgage repayment per month on a $12,000 home, with taxes and based on a 30-year plan, would be about $80 a month. By using 27 per cent of his income a person earning $4,000 a year would qualify, but where will he get the money to meet his other obligations if he has to pay for his mortgage? That is why I say that a longer amortization period is required and by all means a lower interest rate.
If the Minister of Public Works is not in a position today to announce when we may
National Housing Act
expect a bill to readjust the interest rate on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans, the Minister of Finance should at least comment now on the statement made by the Solicitor General to that effect and referred to last evening by the hon. member for Laurier. In order to be fair I would suggest that the act should provide for a special lower rate of interest for people earning less than say $4,000 a year. This particular class of people should not be prevented from owning their homes. For example, on a $12,000 home a rate of interest of even 4f per cent would bring the mortgage payment down to $64 a month from the present $80 a month under a six per cent rate of interest. The Minister of Finance has never missed a chance to take full credit for the releasing of money and the reduction in the interest rate by the Bank of Canada. Now that the discount rate of the Bank of Canada has reached a new low, now that, as reported yesterday, the Bank of Canada discount rate has been reduced to 1.79 per cent from 1.88 per cent just a week ago, there is no reason why the Minister of Finance could not introduce a bill immediately reducing accordingly the rate of interest now charged by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Only then will the act work effectively in the Atlantic provinces, and only by a longer amortization period and a lower interest rate will our low income bracket wage earners be in a position to take full advantage of this legislation.
