Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks, I wish to congratulate you most sincerely on your appointment to the position you occupy.
Sanitary housing is essential to the progress of a people such as ours. Times are no more when people are willing to be crowded into substandard houses which breed disease and cause serious social problems.
It is therefore inconceivable that this government should not participate more actively in slum clearance. I am myself a councillor of the city of Montreal in addition to representing here a heavily populated Montreal constituency where the housing problem is crucial. However, our municipalities cannot afford to clear slums without running into serious financial difficulties.
The present government, speaking through its candidates in the last election, promised help to municipalities in as large a measure

National Housing Act
as possible. Is it not time that the government keep its word by helping the municipalities to clear these slums? And this government aid can only be given in the form of financial assistance.
I regret that this has not been put to more use, in this connection, by the government. The central government will not solve the problem of housing by voting only $350,000,000 in order to facilitate new loans. In a constituency like mine, where families are attached to their parish, people are not ready to move away from one place to another which might not suit them. What should be done is to tear down and then rebuild on the same spot so that our fine families, attached to the constituency, will not have to move elsewhere.
I respectfully suggest that the central government should contribute at least 75 to 80 per cent of the cost of slum clearance to our municipalities. In addition to helping improve the housing situation, it would assist in solving the unemployment problem in each of our localities while giving our workers the opportunity of working to give our area a new look and keeping its population.
That is an important aspect that I wish to stress, and which I do not find in the bill now under consideration. I will vote for the bill but I find it incomplete.
Mr. Chairman, I urge the Minister of Public Works to give serious consideration to the few remarks I just made and to act on them as far as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I will be brief since I am in favour of the resolution under discussion at this time. I regret however that the amount put at the disposal of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not any greater than it is. I would have preferred to vote $250,000,000 more to this body.
Another shortcoming in this proposed resolution is that the interest rate at 6 per cent is too high. The federal government should be able to lend money on easier terms than anybody else. It should be able to bring down the interest rate from 6 per cent to 5 per cent for a period of 20 to 25 years; otherwise the poor low salaried individual will have to pay his own home twice over before managing to own it completely. By this time he will have to buy another house since the first will be half broken down.
Moreover I think that the National Housing Act should be improved in order to foster

better co-operation between municipalities and provincial and federal governments with regard to the buying of land. The greatest injustice at this time is the fabulous price that people have to pay for a little lot of 50 feet by 100 feet or 50 feet by 80 feet, at prices running up to $2,000, $2,500, $3,000. Buyers are at the mercy of clever operators who bought up this land at a low price and make fortunes reselling it to low wage earners.
Moreover, agreements between municipalities, provincial governments and the federal government should provide for the servicing of land by the installation of sewers, water and sidewalks. The cost of this work should be shared by the three levels of government. With a policy such as this, houses would be more within the means of prospective buyers. To my mind it is the only way to encourage our Canadian fellow-citizens to be more Canadian, to be happier to live in Canada and also, at the same time spare those who work hard for low pay the necessity of paying rentals of $100 or more. Furthermore it would encourage them to recognize the advantages of democracy.
In conclusion I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to be kind enough to consider the suggestions I have just made. I believe that the fact of increasing the amount of assistance to our population in connection with the purchase of lots and the installation of municipal services, without exacting small fortunes from the prospective buyers, would be to the greatest advantage not only of the municipalities but of the provincial and federal government as well. In fact, the price of lots and the cost of municipal services represent more than a third of the value of the property. A simple calculation is convincing enough. It comes to about $30 to $35 a month for 25 years.
I think-and I believe that all hon. members will agree with me-that it is preferable to sacrifice millions of dollars to build houses which will be useful to our fellow-citizens than to give them help in the manner here proposed. In fact, the way things are now, it is no longer unemployment insurance but rather a kind of direct relief, or dole, such as that of the years 1930 to 1935.
It would be much better to spend more money so that our workers, instead of getting token payments of $20 to $30 a week while doing nothing may have a job allowing them to live decently. This would be to the advantage of all Canadians and would stimulate the development of our country.

I support this resolution but I would do it with more enthusiasm if it were modified, because I believe that $350 million will not be enough for the construction of the housing units now required. This would give work to our people and would be much better than forcing them to be satisfied with unemployment insurance tokens which do not provide them with the money necessary to meet their own needs and the needs of their family.
I therefore hope that this resolution will be carried as soon as possible to the advantage of all the citizens of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, certainly all Canadians are very pleased at the attention that housing in Canada is receiving, because I think we all agree that the state of our housing has a considerable influence on the Canadian way of life. Sociologists, I suppose, would say that a great percentage of delinquency is directly related to environment which, in turn, is directly related to substandard housing conditions. We are certainly pleased to find that the government has seen fit, in a few short months, to make several commitments towards improving housing conditions in Canada.
We have seen that, in those countries where housing has been available to both the low income groups and others in a position to better afford housing, the way of life has been greatly influenced. Personally, I am not sure just what other measures are going to be taken in the housing field this session. We have hopes, and have been led to expect, that there will be something further to this measure we have before us because there are many other aspects of the housing question to be considered. We are aware also that in addition to making this money available the federal government, provincial governments and municipalities are going to have to take an increasing interest in housing conditions in our country. We have found that the sources previously available for financing housing are no longer available and the government has had to become more and more interested in housing. One of the problems, outside of the fact we need to make money available to potential home owners, is the fact that in the past we have tied the ability to obtain a loan to the applicant's level of income. This has worked untold hardships upon those in the low income groups.
Mention has been made of the difficulty people experience in buying homes in small
National Housing Act
communities such as towns or villages where the standard of housing is not up to that of our major cities. We have many towns that have housing developments which central mortgage and housing considers substandard but which are, in fact, all the people can afford to provide for themselves. These people face great difficulty in obtaining even that type of housing. We see them going to lenders who ask exorbitant interest rates, and even in cases where they are buying under the auspices of the National Housing Act they have to borrow the amount necessary for the down payment from private lending companies. These people, many of whom are in the low income or medium income groups, find it impossible to pay the rent required for a house that will satisfy their needs, and at the same time save enough money for any type of down payment. I think some consideration must be given to the government purchasing houses and renting them on a basis under which an individual may elect to buy the house at the end of a three-year period.
One of our major problems concerns young married couples. It would appear that a young married couple, having two or three children, are in a worse financial position than they probably will be at any other time in their existence. During the recent election we heard a great many promises made, some of them with respect to newly married couples. I think one of the places where these promises could be implemented quite satisfactorily would be in the field of housing. It is a fact that a young business executive or a young employee in a factory, particularly if he is married, is just starting his life and will be continuing to learn to fit himself for the higher positions which he will later enjoy.
While he is earning this lower rate he may need a two, three or even a four bedroom house and at that time his earning power will certainly be much less than it will be in his later life. He will not have the same necessity in later life to get money of this sort for he will be in a better position to afford adequate housing.
I think some consideration should be given to balancing payments somewhat along the lines of business insurance, where you pay a very low premium at the start with increases from time to time. In that case there is the question of the age requirement, while in housing there would be the requirement of the earning power of the mortgagee, which earning power would of course increase. I believe some such arrangement would enable

National Housing Act
our young people to supply their families with a much more satisfactory type of housing, particularly in cases where there are both boys and girls in the family, and where they could be supplied with separate bedrooms or at least adequate provision could be made according to the family's special needs. This in turn would do something to help our small towns where there is a distinct need today for the improvement in facilities for bringing up many of our children. Such a measure, I believe, would do much to correct many of the faults evident in our suburban housing projects.
There is another problem, so far as housing is concerned, and that is with respect to the mortgages which, under national housing, now run from $9,000 to $10,000 and even up to $16,000 per home. It is true that these are very nice houses which, according to the economists, would be suitable for a group having an income of between $4,000 and $5,000 per year. We are, of course, all aware that in the average wage-earning community in Canada the family income does not run that high in the normal course and it would appear that certain houses which were built for wartime needs are now increasing in value from their original $5,000 price to approximately $10,000 to $12,000 per house. If we were to revert to this type of low cost home building we might do much to assist many of the communities not now in a position to take advantage of national housing.
There is another problem under the National Housing Act which again arises from the young married couple becoming able to build a house but deciding, in this case, to do so out of income. They start with $1,000, put in a basement and finally, by borrowing from their friends and sacrificing everything else for a year or more, are able to put up the four walls. Then they find that before they can raise any kind of mortgage they are going to have to provide for the sheathing and other things all at the same time. They find they must borrow $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000 before they can complete the rudimentary necessities in their house so that they can move in and take advantage of the saving in rent. I know of many couples in my own area who have gone to people to raise small mortgages and who have been asked from 11 per cent to 12 per cent interest. Their banks and legal counsel have advised them that there must be sheathing on the house and it would not be possible to take a mortgage on a house covered with tar paper. They then discover they might as well have taken a mortgage, put up the sheathing and a satisfactory type of roof on the house and put in the plumbing and electricity in the first

place. They would not then have needed to borrow money at these exorbitant rates.
I believe there are occasions when very small sums of money could be advanced under national housing to help people in these circumstances without the strict specifications which the act now requires to be fulfilled. Such loans would be a very small part of the value of the house and would suit the needs of the many people in Canada who do not believe it is a satisfactory state of affairs when we mortgage our souls before we can own anything at all. They believe they should pay as they go along and I certainly think something should be done to help these people.
There is another complaint in connection with housing in general and that is the matter of inspection. We have seen many homes built where the rudimentary regulations as to good housing practices have not been enforced. We have seen lumber used that has never been dried, lumber that has been taken off the saw and sold to a contractor and he then puts it in a house. We have all seen cases, particularly with cupboards, where everything was nicely painted when the person moved in but very soon they could pretty nearly put the cups and saucers in the cupboards without even opening the doors. While it is not necessarily inferior material which is being used it certainly would not meet suitable building requirements with respect to its processing. We have seen door jambs with large cracks in them and many other conditions which are not satisfactory to a young home owner, who has not necessarily the ability to know whether he is getting full value when he buys a $10,000 house or whether he is getting only $6,000 value for his money. I think we should be very careful in protecting our people against some of the wiles of the contractors which they are currently practising upon us, the unsuspecting public.
Another problem is the matter of a suitable guarantee against disaster. We are all very interested in the youth of Canada being able to provide suitable housing for their families, but I think the government could legitimately require the inclusion of an insurance clause in these mortgages, particularly those of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which would guarantee that the family would not lose its home as a result of unemployment in an area which might be classed a disaster unemployment area, or because of the death of the breadwinner of the family. In the case of unemployment, payments could be suspended so that foreclosure would not take place and the family would not lose its equity.
I am sure the minister is familiar with this problem and also with another point

which I would now like to raise. That is with respect to the third classification under the housing act in respect to mining communities and other communities which are developing across the country such as Blind River, Elliot Lake and Bancroft. I am sure we are all very sympathetic with miners who are moving into these communities and we can very plainly see the results when the industry supporting the area falls on hard times. I can think of towns which were built up when mining was in its heyday, towns such as Kirkland Lake and others in the immediate vicinity, when it was expedient for everybody to build as is now happening in Blind River and Elliot Lake.
I think some consideration should be given to the future of these people who are in many cases engaged in an industry-and I refer particularly to the uranium industry- over which the government is going to exercise more and more control. I think we are all aware that if some day we should throw the contracts for uranium on to the open market many of these mines would have to close down and the communities which depend on them would go out of existence. I think that at the same time as we advance money through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build homes in these areas we should give some guarantee that the young miners and their families who put their savings into these homes will have a house which is worth something 20 or 30 years from now.
We have houses in the town of Matachewan which 10 years ago were worth between $8,000 and $10,000 but which are available today for two or three thousand dollars. As I say, some consideration should be given to the position of these people.
Again, I should be interested to know what further housing legislation the government has in mind for 1958. According to my interpretation of the speech from the throne there is more to come in the housing field, and we certainly hope this is the case. Particular consideration should be given to guaranteeing the position of those people who have been unemployed for eight or nine months-and there are many people in this position in my own area-who are now faced with having to go to a bank, or to somebody else, in order to obtain money to protect their investment on a very short term basis. I doubt whether a third mortgage will be available, or whether it will be worth the paper it is written on, and in these circumstances I think the government should give some consideration to their difficulties. I believe the minister is sympathetic and I hope he will keep this question in mind if there are to be other
National Housing Act
developments in the housing field this year, because in northern Ontario, in particular, we are finding that a great deal of distress has developed among people who are buying homes in the new developments there; they are not sure that they will be able to recover even the money they have already spent on their housing.
We think, also, that the minister would be well advised to examine the over-all picture with regard to housing with a view to entering the housing field not only on a mortgage basis but also with respect to low rental housing so that people who need accommodation today, particularly multi-bedroom housing, could rent their homes and relinquish them when they were no longer needed, passing them on to others who had need of this particular accommodation while they themselves rented homes more suited to their new needs.

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to speak on the resolution because I was under the impression that there was a certain haste about this matter because of the necessity of getting the bill before the Senate. I now understand, however, that the other place has now taken a recess and that the minister is not averse to a leisurely discussion on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no. The Senate is meeting today at four o'clock, and I am hopeful we can get royal assent this afternoon. If we do not get the bill over by that time I am afraid it will be impossible.

I will do what I can to limit my remarks. I am sure the house would not want to miss my words of wisdom. Mr. Chairman I might bring to your attention that I understand the Hansard staff have great difficulty in hearing us at this end of the house and it would be most unfortunate if they failed to hear every word we utter. Perhaps you would have that taken up.
I may say that the Minister of Public Works and 1 were at one time engaged in the first immense interest-free housing development which was ever undertaken by the Canadian people. I refer to the time when we were both digging dugouts together in front of Ypres. I think that was the first interest-free housing development by Canada.
I must say I was interested in listening to the minister's summary of the legislation, and the summary of recent happenings since the government took office. I am very glad he gave that summary because it was quite informative as to past and recent events, and also as to the present proposals. We support this resolution, as some of my colleagues have mentioned, although we think it is completely

National Housing Act
inadequate to meet all the housing necessities of the Canadian people. When the minister began to speak I really thought he had become a convert to public financing of housing in Canada. However when he was concluding his speech I thought he sounded like a bride who had flirted with an idea and then broken off the engagement.
I should like to bring one or two matters to the attention of the minister before going on to deal with C.C.F. policy with respect to housing. I may say that some of my friends are interested in the lumber industry, and I want to tell the minister that a good many firms in the lumber industry have been producing lately with very little margin; some have even been producing at less than cost in order to keep their staffs employed, though at the same time retail lumber prices across Canada have dropped very little. I think this is something which will bear inquiry, the increasing spread between the cost of lumber at the mill and the purchase price paid by the consumer. I have had this matter brought to my attention by a number of people from Saskatchewan who are interested in building and who are amazed to hear of the low price for which lumber is being sold by the lumber manufacturers in B.C.
I am very interested about the proposed housing redevelopment in Trail, and very glad the government made a grant toward the necessary survey. I hope the result will mean a satisfactory co-operative arrangement among the federal, provincial and municipal governments so that the present situation will be improved in the near future. I also wish to express my appreciation of the minister's attention to the Sunningdale veterans housing development. I am not going into the details but this is a matter which I had brought to the attention of the former government on several occasions and I appreciate very much the prompt way in which the minister tackled this rather thorny question and the co-operation he received from his officials. I had a letter two or three days ago from the president of the committee representing the veterans concerned expressing their satisfaction with the basis for the settlement of the problem.
Previous speakers mentioned the difficulties involved in the obtaining of loans in small towns and villages. I wish the minister and his officials would investigate that question. I have run into similar situations on a number of occasions and I am sure it is much more difficult to obtain these loans in the smaller places than the minister is aware of at present. I urge him to give the matter consideration and make it the subject of further investigation.

The question of inspection was also mentioned and this is a matter which in my opinion also requires investigation. I have seen some rather shabby examples of poor inspection over the years. I believe the minister has knowledge of one house that passed inspection by one of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation inspectors which I think personally was a damned disgrace. I mean that in the limited theological sense, Mr. Prime Minister. Inside of six months the cement began to powder off the basement walls and the plaster in the bedrooms, the dining room and in other places had begun to fall down. On the whole it was a pretty poor show and I think greater attention should be paid to inspection. I am not saying this has happened frequently but when it occurs it is a serious matter to the persons directly concerned.
Having said all the nice things I can possibly say at this moment, I want now to say a few words with respect to the failure of the present housing legislation to meet the needs of many Canadians. We in the C.C.F. consider that the provision of housing is a major responsibility of government. We look upon it as something in the nature of public utilities, the development of power, the provision of irrigation and conservation policies and things of that sort. This is the provision of legislation to conserve human beings and their dignity. We in this group are sometimes accused of having little regard for the value and dignity of the individual but on the contrary we base our whole outlook toward life on the concept of the great worth of the individual and the desirability of preserving his integrity and dignity. We believe it is necessary to have good housing if we are going to have good Canadians. We have to have good houses if we are going to have good homes. We must have good homes if we are going to build good Canadian citizens. Unfortunately at the present time we have large numbers of very poor homes in Canada. One does not have to go very far from these parliament buildings in order to And some slum dwellings in this area which are a disgrace at this stage in our history. We are not suggesting that we should do something for nothing but we feel the state should use its good offices to the full to ensure that each Canadian who is willing and able to work and accept his responsibilities with regard to debt obligation will have a modern and decent home in which to raise his family. I think I am quite right in saying that at this time the majority of Canadians do not have that opportunity.
To confirm that statement I want to read some official figures taken from the dominion bureau of statistics and taxation statistics.

The average income of borrowers under the National Housing Act in 1956 was $5,312. By the third quarter of 1957-the latest period for which figures are available when these calculations were made-the average income of borrowers was nearly $6,000, or $5,943 to be exact. It is interesting to observe that 91 per cent of those who filed income tax returns in 1955-the latest year for which taxation statistics are available when these calculations were made-earned annual incomes of less than $5,000. That is according to the taxation statistics of the Department of National Revenue published in 1957. Only 204 out of a total of 47,593 borrowers under the National Housing Act, or four-tenths of 1 per cent, were in the $3,000 or less annual income bracket in 1956. By the third quarter of 1957 those earning $3,000 or less comprised only one-tenth of 1 per cent of borrowers. Sixty-two per cent of all persons who filed income tax returns in 1955 earned annual incomes of less than $3,000.
Those figures in my opinion clearly indicate the inability of large numbers of Canadians to secure loans under our present housing legislation. Moreover, under the housing regulations an approved lender, I am told, is required to obtain special approval from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in making a loan to the applicant if the debt service is more than 27 per cent of the applicant's income. This means that at the present time, for example, a borrower must have an annual income of $3,450 to qualify for a $9,000 loan on a house. According to income tax returns filed in 1955, 73.1 per cent or about three out of four Canadian income earners made less than $3,500. This clearly demonstrates the inadequacy of the present housing legislation. We can contrast that with the huge amounts we spend on defence expenditures. We heard recently of the expenditure of $200 million on aircraft that may be obsolete very quickly. We all know it is not the fault of any individual that a great deal of this vast defence expenditure is on equipment which becomes obsolete very quickly under present world conditions. However we in this group feel that if we can afford these vast defence expenditures we certainly should be able to afford the expenditure required to provide the necessary housing of adequate standards required by Canadians who are willing and able to work and accept their responsibilities. I am not one who is in favour of giving something for nothing.
I have no regard for a healthy lazy person and would not raise a hand to help such a person if he were in good health and capable of providing for himself and I believe that
National Housing Act
view is generally accepted in this group. However, we are anxious to give all Canadians the opportunity of obtaining the housing they require. On that account we in the C.C.F. have a policy with regard to housing which we believe would go a long way toward meeting the situation at least under present circumstances. I propose to read that policy to the committee so it will be on the record:
In order to change this deplorable housing situation, a C.C.F. government would:
(a)	Issue loans, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, directly to the borrower and set up a special revolving fund (a fund that completes in time the circuit between loans and payments) for that purpose:
(b)	Make such loans bear a fixed interest of 2 per cent:
That, I understand, would cover the cost of administration and make a reasonable allowance for possible losses and so on. It simply means in effect that we would provide the loans at cost. I continue:
(c)	Make the amount of the loan 90 per cent of the lending value up to $12,000.
This aspect of C.C.F. housing policy which the C.C.F. have been urging for some years was finally adopted by the Conservative government in the last session of parliament. I continue:
(d)	Increase the amortization period to 30 years instead of 25;
(e)	Establish a rental subsidy fund to provide low rental housing for Canadians in the lower income brackets who cannot afford to buy or build houses, even under the most favourable conditions;
(f)	Make grants to the provinces to be turned over to the municipalities for the purpose of constructing schools and other public facilities which are a heavy expense, and often indeed, a prohibitive one, on the municipality undertaking a new housing project. In this way, the municipalities would be able to take advantage of the provisions of the housing act.
Those are our proposals with respect to a housing policy under the present circumstances. All of our group are intensely interested in this question but I wish to make a personal suggestion. This is an extremely serious problem to all low income earners. In my opinion this is a problem that should be tackled as a result of a thorough examination of the question as the result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, the municipalities, those supplying materials, the construction industry and the labour groups engaged in the construction industry. This is something that everyone has to make a contribution toward in an effort to design a policy which will make it possible for those low-income earners who are denied decent housing at the present time under present legislation to acquire houses. All these people should

National Housing Act
get together, investigate the problem and cooperate in what I would consider would be a vast and worth-while national program and objective.

In that case I can leave the majority of my intended remarks for a future occasion when the opportunity will arise. The only thing I should like to say at the present time has to do with the point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He referred to the cost involved in building one airplane for our defence. On many occasions we have found that as soon as we have spent the money the particular plane has almost immediately become obsolete and we have had to proceed to build something new and better. I was wondering whether as a nation we could not look at our housing program in a somewhat similar light.
What do we do with these airplanes when they become obsolete? Do we keep on using them knowing that they are obsolete and dangerous or do we scrap them and get something that is worth while? If that principle were carried into our housing program I think it would give us a good idea of what should be done with regard to housing. Some hon. members may recall that during the last session I made reference to some of my personal experiences as a municipal fire-fighter both in answering calls to fires and in making inspections of houses on a door-to-door basis with the purpose in mind of eliminating causes of fires before they actually happened and trying to close the door before the horse was stolen. I think that is one aspect of housing that should be pursued with all vigour.
To give one illustration, houses built as recently as 20 years ago were ideal examples of modern house construction at that time, but let us consider the number of electrical appliances that have come into common use in the last 20 years and we will see what some of the problems are. At the time these houses were built they were wired in what was considered to be a proper and adequate manner sufficient to handle all requirements at that time and possibly in the then foreseeable future. But because of the development of appliances in a very short period of time we now find that what was adequate 20, 10 or even 5 years ago is today a danger to life and limb.
I believe that is something that should be taken into consideration and watched very carefully in the construction of the houses that we hope will be built under the measure we are dealing with today. I hope that the inspectors and the people in responsible

Mr. Chairman, while listening to the debate on this resolution, I thought that certain things should be said, particularly at a stage where we are afforded much more latitude than when we are discussing the bill itself.
As the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) said the other day, we have found that, since the adoption of this legislation, i.e. since 1954-which in no way reflects the attitude of the present government-the main beneficiaries of the act have been the large corporations, particularly large contracting firms in metropolitan areas and the large centres of this country, where profits, while legitimate if you wish, are paid by the small buyer who needs a house.
I wondered if there were no means of making government loans more accessible to the small buyer, because the main objective of the government since 1954, an objective which, to my knowledge, has not changed today, has been to give easy access to home ownership to the man of limited means. We are about to lose an item of wealth. In cities like Montreal, for instance, property is centralized in the hands of a few individuals and the large majority of residents are tenants. When house ownership is thus centralized among a few owners there is always the danger that we shall have no slum clearance, but an increase of slum areas, because the large real estate owner merely wants to get a profit out of the housing he rents and is hardly interested in the appearance, and even in the sanitary conditions of these lodgings.
Now I believe that the government should try to make home ownership more readily accessible to the small people than to large contractors who are merely interested in acquiring property for purposes of speculation.
As one of the previous speakers was saying-I have forgotten who it was-the main people whom the government should try to interest in home ownership, should be young married couples who have their whole lives in front of them, who plan to raise a family, and who will need a home, not only for a few months but for years. They are the ones we should help take advantage of these loans. Above all, they should be advised not to build one-family units, which in times of recession become a danger since they have to keep on making their regular payments, pay their taxes, amortize their mortgage and pay the

National Housing Act
interest, which is all very difficult tor them to do in the circumstances. But if we helped them build two-tamily units, so that they could count on someone else to help them meet their obligations during hard times it would help them keep their property.
In Hull, a wonderful residential district was built with the help of these mortgage loans. Then, all of a sudden, a zoning law was enacted whereby two-family units were forbidden. For a certain difficult period these people had great trouble making their payments, so much so that many of them had to put their house up for sale. Then, those who are buying these houses will soon be in the same fix.
There are always a lot of people who do not wish to become owners but who nonetheless want to live in a decent house, and this helps the owner pay for his house and keep it.
In order to achieve such a purpose, I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) was right in saying this morning that in this age of technology, the department responsible for these loans should have experts study the method of building a decent house at a low price, a practical house which could be resold at a still cheaper price. This is in line with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) to the effect that some arrangement should be made between the federal, provincial and municipal governments in order that individuals may be prevented from buying a farm at such a low price as to enable them to parcel them out in lots for resale at $1,200, $1,500 and even $3,000, which lots might have cost only $50 or $60.
I am not criticizing the act, as I am in favour of it, but I think it could be improved. If the department would buy the land, subdivide it and put the lots up for sale, larg contractors would not be afforded the opportunity of making high profits, and the small borrowers would be the ones to benefit.
Now there is the matter of interest rate. The interest rate, which is 6 per cent, is of course too high. I pointed this out at the time it was raised, two years ago. I said then that the interest rate was too high, and I repeat it today.
That is the way I have felt about it all along, and always will.
We often have occasion to criticize the government of the province of Quebec, and perhaps with reason, but the government has achieved things which I admire, notably its policy of helping the small home owner by refunding to him about 3 per cent on the

interest he has had to pay <5n his building loan. Under the National Housing Act, the interest rate is 6 per cent.
It is still being claimed, as it was at the time, that the purpose of the 6 per cent interest rate was to encourage lending institutions and banks to grant loans. Well, I think that when the loan is granted by the government itself, through one of its departments, the money should be loaned at no more than 3 per cent. When the loan is made through a bank, the federal government should pay the difference between 3 and 6 per cent, so as to help those who need it most. In fact the object of all this legislation is not to encourage the making of huge profits, but to foster home ownership, and if we want to encourage people to own their own homes, we must help them to do so.
Everybody agrees that no one should pay more than the equivalent of three years' salary for his house. A man who earns $3,000 should not buy a property of more than $9,000 for he runs the risk of losing it. Consequently, if the interest rate were reduced, he would have a wider choice. This is especially true of the man who has or is likely to have a large family; he could then afford to buy a home in which to raise his family under normal conditions.
Somebody spoke a moment ago about slums in Montreal. The fact is that there are slums in every part of this country, and the object of this legislation is precisely to get rid of slums.
I am convinced that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) means well when he asks the house to vote a further amount of $300 million; we are going to vote this amount. I think each and every member wishes to comply with his request. However, I hope the suggestions we are offering to improve the act itself will be seriously considered by the hon. minister, because we do not make them with the idea of slowing up the passage of the bill, but to give easier access to home ownership to the small man in this country.
