speechtext:
I am dealing with the statement as it appears in Hansard and, of course, if my hon. friend wants to correct it he is free to do so, but I know when he dealt with this question he certainly interjected a very strong political note. I detected it from the start; of course he started off in a very friendly manner as he always does but he waxed political after a little while and perhaps succeeded in interrupting to an extent the progress of his legislation. That is why I objected as I do now to these two statements and the point I am trying to make is that we today have the Minister of Finance talking easy money and the Minister of Public Works, in charge of housing, practising tight money.
The mortage rate, as I understand it and as I am informed, for home ownership under the National Housing Act was established at 6 per cent. We established that rate over a year ago and it has remained at 6 per cent ever since. I understand that the formula when establishing the rate is that it should not exceed the interest rate on long-term government bonds by more than 2\ per cent. Long-term government bonds have now fallen off and I believe their rate is under 3 per cent, which means the National Housing Act rate could go down to 5J per cent or perhaps even 5J per cent.
My colleague, the member for Hull, made a point in that he suggested perhaps a compromise or an arrangement might be made between the provincial and federal governments such as obtains in certain parts of Canada today, but we on this side of the house believe that the fall in the interest rates is the result of a decline in confidence and a decline in investment since my hon.

friends opposite took office, and that when there are no alternative investments the lending institutions would lend at a lower rate than the present one. I know it is not necessary to point this out to the minister but I would like to put on record one fact and that is that every one per cent of interest that must be paid on the principal of the mortgage substantially increases the amount of income which the prospective home owner must have in order to be accepted as an approved buyer of the mortgaged property.
The change in the regulations recently adopted has alleviated the situation to some extent but it cannot alter the fact that interest costs are the major items which enter into the calculations.
The regulations require, broadly speaking, that the income of the prospective buyer shall be of such amount that 27 per cent will cover the interest on the mortgage, the amortization of principal and the taxes, so it follows that if the interest rate is higher than it need be a number of buyers with limited means are excluded. Thus a reduction of $50 in the interest cost would reduce the amount of income required by nearly $200. A lower rate offers obvious advantages in that it would increase the number of persons who could qualify as approved buyers.
A great deal has been said in the course of the discussion with respect to housing development and construction in smaller centres and something has also been said of urban redevelopment. There is at present a great need for redevelopment in our cities to rehabilitate blighted or substandard areas. Very little has been done in this field in Canada up to now because such projects are extremely costly. Municipalities are hesitant to embark upon such programs, either because they do not know that they can receive federal assistance for such a purpose, or because they feel that the provision of the National Housing Act in this respect does not go far enough.
We think positive steps should be taken to inform the municipalities more adequately about the federal assistance available to them for redevelopment projects. Moreover, we on this side of the house would improve the provisions of the act, particularly sections 36 and 23, so as to encourage municipalities to take greater initiative in this field than they have done in the past.
At the present time section 36 of the National Housing Act provides that the federal government can undertake in collaboration with the provincial governments or their agencies-that is to say the municipalities-projects for the acquisition and

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
development of land for housing purposes and for the construction of houses.
The federal contribution to the financing of these development projects is 75 per cent of the cost, therefore the federal government does not share in the cost of such items as roads, sewage and waterworks related to those projects. We should like to see a provision in the act which would include those works which are essential parts of any redevelopment project in the cost shared by the federal government.
There is also another section of the act- section 23-providing for federal assistance to the municipalities to help in the clearance, replanning, rehabilitation and modernization of blighted or substandard areas. The slum clearance work contemplated under this section is merely a preliminary step toward redevelopment or rebuilding projects defined in section 36. However, the federal contribution to the financing of this preliminary work is only 50 per cent of the cost. We would like to see the federal contribution as provided under section 23 of the act increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent so as to make it similar to that provided under section 36, because the work contemplated in those two sections constitutes two phases of the same programs.
Finally, these sections of the act, apply only at present to residential housing projects. In several cases, however, the blighted or substandard areas should not be used for housing purposes but should be transformed into commercial districts or into municipal parks. We should like to see abolished the present restrictions on the nature of redevelopment projects which qualify for federal assistance and would extend such assistance to redevelopment projects for commercial and other purposes as well as housing where this is advisable.
Then there is the question of land costs. I am pleased to see that the minister intends to give this subject some thought and consideration. I realize, as he does himself, that the crown corporation is certainly not directly responsible for this situation, but it has a particular interest in the problem in that if the costs continue to rise the position in so far as the crown company is concerned will become more and more difficult. I am sure that if an investigation were made into these costs by the president of the corporation, either alone, or through his officials or in co-operation with the municipalities and the provinces, it might be possible to find some method of reducing costs in this field.
There was also the question of appraisals.
I hope the minister will find it possible to say a word on this subject. Perhaps he has done
National Housing Act
so, but I did not notice. Toward the end of my remarks yesterday I asked whether he could not say something on that subject. Perhaps if he does not wish to deal with it now he could reserve his remarks until we come to consider the bill. I just wanted to make these remarks not in any desire to hold up the legislation but with one desire only, namely, to be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In reply to the last subject raised by the hon. member for Laurier, we shall try to arrange for a discussion at as early a date as possible on the estimates. Since the hon. gentleman and I had a brief exchange about the number of starts, I have received the figures from the officials for the months January to April inclusive. Last year-1957-there were 12,816; this year, 1958, they are almost doubled at 24,946.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the minister the figures for 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid not.
Has the minister the figures for the Atlantic provinces for the same period?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

Perhaps the minister would care to comment on the subject I was dealing with yesterday. Is it not a fact that the high rate of construction during March, April, May and June of last year used up the great bulk of the private money that was available and thus necessitated the present steps which the government has taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I believe the statement I made in my speech yesterday afternoon was correct, and that housing in Canada was falling off in the early part of last year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The facts are exactly to the contrary.

How can the minister
justify the present rate of 6 per cent when this rate was established while the interest rate of the Bank of Canada was 4.3 per cent, and it is now down, as announced yesterday, to 1.79 per cent? Furthermore, how can he reconcile the statement which was made by the Prime Minister in Calgary, as reported in the Calgary Herald of March 15, that his government had put $300 million into house building with his present policy, and with the claim that the government had reduced the interest rate from 4.3 per cent to 2.89 per cent, which it was at that date. The government is taking credit for reducing interest rates generally. Why not apply this to mortgage loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?

National Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: The Prime Minister certainly tried to connect the new money for house building with the rate of interest current at the time. He certainly tried to connect those two things, making a political question out of it, and that is clearly indicated by the statement I have just taken from the Calgary Herald.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the rates to which the Prime Minister was referring were a different set of rates, not the rate based, as we have to calculate our rate, on section 4 of the act.
The Prime Minister certainly did not make that clear in his statement. He had some other ideas at the time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have a question to ask but I can leave it until we come to the bill.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Green thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-10, to amend the National Housing Act, 1954.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall this bill be read the second time?
Now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: By leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: the second reading of the bill.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Advances out of the C.R.F. to make loans and pay losses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, earlier I put on the record some figures having to do with house building activity in 1957 and I believe the minister has that table before him. In view of the rise in the number of starts from January to June 1957 would the minister say whether that is not some indication that private loans were gradually being forced out of the field?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no indication whatever that private loans were forced out by the small home loan plan. Actually it was brought in to fill a gap which had been left by the withdrawal of the lending institutions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before this measure was put in the form of a resolution what was the percentage vis-a-vis government money and private enterprise money in the field of housing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not have those figures with me. I could get them from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and give them to you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have no intention of holding up the measure because of that but I would be interested, and I am sure the committee would be, as to the progress that was made in the approximate amount of money invested by the government in the field of housing and that invested by private enterprise, let us say in 1956, 1957 and the first quarter of 1958 or that part of 1958 for which the minister has figures. I take it the minister has not that information available today.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would be glad to get that information for the hon. member.

Would the minister explain to the committee the procedure in transferring moneys from the consolidated revenue fund to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and whether it is transferred as a lump sum or as the corporation requires the funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is transferred as the corporation requires the funds.

In view of the statement the minister made last fall when he asked this house for an additional amount of $150 million and when he said this sum would be used partly to help maritime residents to take advantage of the scheme, and also in view of a statement which he made at a later date to the effect that the money was there available and if demands were not made responsibility for that rested with the people in the provinces, could the minister not give us an indication now as to how many people in the Atlantic provinces have taken advantage of this additional amount of money which parliament has voted under the National Housing Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There was not the same use made of the small home loan plan in the Atlantic provinces. There was not the building of homes going on there and the demand for this money was not as great in that area.
Can the minister give any indication as to the amount that was used in the Atlantic provinces? Was it 5 per cent, 10 per cent or less of the amount made available?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not a question of the
amount that was made available. The whole sum was made available all over Canada. Actually the amount loaned in the hon. member's province of New Brunswick was $1,867,245.46 under the small home loan plan.
What period does that cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is throughout the whole period of operation of the plan since last August. The number of housing units in New Brunswick was 191.
Could the minister give the same figures for Newfoundland? How many houses have been financed out of public funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There were 64 units in Newfoundland involving a total of $717,279. I would point out, however, that in Newfoundland the city of St. John's has had a greater benefit proportionately under the federal-provincial low rental plan than any other centre in Canada.
But that is not under this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, on May 13 in reply to a question I asked the minister said that the fund has not been exhausted and there still remains a small amount. I wonder if the minister could indicate in round figures how much money is in the fund at the present time that has not yet been used. I have another question that is related to the fund not having been exhausted. I believe it was yesterday the minister indicated in his remarks that over the past several months he had to curtail the program first of all in regard to apartment buildings and in the last month in regard to small units. Is the minister able to say how many millions of dollars would have been spent if curtailment of the program had not been necessary. I think the minister will know what I am after. How many housing units were not built that would have been built had there been no curtailment in the program?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The amount committed as of May 9 was $392,073,613. I am not very good
National Housing Act
at mental arithmetic but I am sure the hon. member could calculate much more rapidly than I could just how much that leaves in the fund. It is very nearly $8 million. At the time we suspended the loans under the small home loan plan there were applications for close to $50 million. As I said earlier in the debate approximately 75 per cent of those loans were taken up by the lending institutions and the banks so there is no question of the construction of these homes having been stopped. Once we get these funds we will be able to deal with the applications which have not been taken over by the lending institutions and the banks. I would remind the hon. member, however, that some of these applications may not be acceptable and the applicants may not qualify.

I thank the minister for his answer. Since $50 million worth was on application at the time he had to curtail the plan and 75 per cent of that he believes has been taken up by the lending institutions it means that 25 per cent has been delayed in implementation. This indicates there has been a delay in the construction of 1,750 units assuming they had all been approved.
It is fairly reasonable to say that because the minister on February 1 did not ask parliament for money when the government knew it was going to be running out of money there has been a delay in housing starts to the extent of at least 1,000 units. It is regrettable, and I wish the government had taken advantage of the good will that existed at that time in the house and the anxiety that the house was expressing to supply him with that amount of money so that there would not be an interruption and needless unemployment.
In his answer to my first question he says that I am good in my arithmetic, but he also says $392 million has been expended. At the time we voted the money last year I believe Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had exhausted its funds. So far as I know the government placed the extra $150 million into the fund, which they had authority to do, when they inaugurated this program and for which they did not need the sanction of the house. We then supplied by legislation another $150 million. These two amounts added together mean that the government and parliament put $300 million more into the fund during the time of the Conservative government's tenure of office, and yet he says expenditures reached $392 million. Does this amount of $92 million mean that this money has come back by way of repayments of loans, or where did the money come from?

National Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member is too suspicious. I explained yesterday that the original legislation provided $250 million. About $100 million of that had been spent before we took over, leaving approximately $150 million. That $150 million was allocated largely, not entirely, because it also had to provide for the loans in small centres and for the loans to limited dividend corporations and to primary industry. That $150 million was allocated for the main part to the small home loan plan. Then, when we found that more money would be required we came to the house and asked for it last November. When the last parliament was dissolved there was no indication that we would run out of money before the new parliament was summoned.
What happened was that in the spring months the applications for loans increased by leaps and bounds and at this point I am a little suspicious myself. I think that many of the lending institutions and probably the banks were simply shoving off applications onto the small homes loan plan which should have gone under the insured loan plan under the National Housing Act.
That is exactly what the hon. member for Laurier said.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think they were doing it; I think that is what was happening. We did not expect that that would take place and the money ran out a little earlier than we had expected. We were not trying to deceive the house in any way.
Would the minister care to explain. He has now said the $100 million was exhausted when his government took office. Then $150 million was added to the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No; the $150 million was in the fund. We simply decided it was not being used by the former government for any plan of the type of the small homes loan plan. We initiated this new plan and decided to use the $150 million for that purpose.

Will the minister explain how he could spend $392 million if he had at his disposal only this $150 million and the $150 million that was voted by the House of Commons. Where did the other $92 million come from?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member is not as good at arithmetic as I thought he was. The $100 million had already been spent before we took over. The figure of $392 million-odd includes the $100 million that had been spent before we took over last June.

That answers the question but I do want to clear up the record at least in

my mind and perhaps in the minds of a few other hon. members. The record of the Conservative government house-building program is not $392 million, then. Part of that $392 million had been expended already by the previous government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think any Conservative has claimed that we have provided $392 million. The figures I have always heard are $300 million, which figure is accurate.

Would the minister permit me to ask what is probably a very stupid question? The minister as a lawyer would probably regard it also as a very ignorant question. I looked at the explanatory note very quickly and I could not make out from it whether this was a revolving fund or whether once the loan was repaid to the corporation the money had to be paid back to the government. In other words, I wondered whether the payments on the mortgages as they come back to the corporation can be used for relending? I admit there would not be very much repaid yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a very sensible question; I am somewhat surprised, but it really is.
Then we are both surprised.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: My understanding is that the money is paid back into the corporation.
And can be lent again?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And can be used by it.

Has the minister by chance the amount of the repayments that have been made, the replenishment of the fund that has come about from the repayments? I assume that the $100 million that was lent before the hon. gentleman became a minister was lent over a period of years and that there might have been quite a considerable amount of it repaid. I was just wondering whether he had the figure or whether it was readily available as to how much had been recovered in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I have not that figure but I will be glad to get it for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I go back to the question on starts. In view of table 1, it occurred to me it might be possible for the minister to tell me how many starts were financed by public money in June, for instance, when the peak was reached, and how many by private enterprise? It may be that the minister has the figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think the hon. member will find the answer to his question, at least in part, in table 18. I have not had time to check it but I have had a note from my

officials saying that this information is contained in table 18 on Canadian housing statistics for the last quarter of last year.

I have another question which may also not be a very bright one but I think I might put it to the minister. If I caught the figure that the hon. member for Laurier gave, there were approximately
10,000	starts in June before the present administration took office or just at the time they took office, or before those new loans were initiated, in any event. In other words, all of those starts must have been financed by private money.
That figure of 10,000 has never been reached again in any month since, during which period the government has been making very considerable loans. Therefore it would appear that the peak of private lending was reached in June, that private lending has been going down steadily ever since and that in so far as the figure has been kept up it has been kept up by public lending. I think that is obvious and I think that the minister will agree.
In other words, that would seem to suggest that there has been a falling off in private lending ever since the peak was reached in June, which would seem to confirm what the minister and the hon. member for Laurier both said, that they were a little concerned about the possibility of public lending driving out the private lenders. But my question is a rather different one. I had understood, perhaps not from the Minister of Public Works, that the Minister of Finance had declared that we were in a position of tight money in June and that since this government came in money was easier. It would appear to me that if money was tight there would be less lending for housing and if money became easier there would be more lending for housing. Yet it would seem from the statistics that there was private money to finance 10,000 starts in June and that there has never been private money to finance anything like that number ever since. In the first place, perhaps the minister might say whether he thinks my analysis is correct because we could differ about it, and then he might explain why in this new era of easy money there was less private money available for housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member is not correct. The first breach that was made in the wall of the tight money policy so strongly supported by the former government was the making of $150 million available for housing about the end of August. I think that was the first relaxation of the tight money policy and the real test was whether or not builders across the country could get money for building. I think that it was to
57071-3-I2i
National Housing Act
some extent, perhaps quite largely, difficult for them because the banks were under instructions not to lend money. I really do not believe that the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate can derive very much comfort from the 10,000 figure in June of last year. If he can, perhaps he will feel better but I do not think it proves very much.

I was not looking for comfort from the minister, I was looking for light. Perhaps the minister would not mind my coming back to this point to see if I can get a little light. The minister suggested, and this puzzles me even more, that the making of $150 million available out of the treasury was creating easy money. I had understood from the Minister of Finance and from other members of the government that easy money was created by reducing interest rates and making more money available from private lenders. I thought the hon. gentleman had campaigned against the Social Crediters and not in favour of them. Surely for the government to go into direct lending is not relieving tight money; it is substituting printing presses or something of that sort for the normal operations of the money market.
It does seem to me that the minister should have a better explanation of why it was that after we got into this new era of easy money there was less money available for housing from the private institutions than there was when we were in office and there were 10,000 starts as there were in June with no government lending but all private lending. That is the point that I do not think the minister has explained.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The real comparison should be between the months of June in the respective years. That would tell the story. June, of course, is normally one of the very best months of the year for starting the construction of homes and I think that is the reason the figure was 10,000 for June of last year.
I would be very much surprised if it is not
20,000	in June of 1958.

I think the minister has an interesting point. I would not be at all surprised if he might be right but I wonder whether 10,000 of that figure will be represented by private lending resulting from the easy money or whether most of it will not be as a result of this direct government lending. That is my point. What I was trying to find out was what the minister really meant by this easy money having produced more housing because it would appear from the statistics to have produced less.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the minister's answer to a question about collections. He said that there was a

National Housing Act
revolving fund within Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If so, I presume it is a very small revolving fund. But over a period of years and in view of the investment by the corporation in housing there must be an increasing sum available from loan collections. Has the minister any idea as to what the amount of collections would be last year, which money would be available to be reinvested in new housing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not got that figure. It will be going up, of course, as time goes on and the mortgage repayments start to come in. The hon. member knows that they are comparatively small in the earlier years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister Will not mind if I come back to the interest rate again because he and I practically put the same statement on the record a moment ago. However, there is just one discrepancy which I should like to see cleared up. I said that the rate had been established some time ago at six per cent and that my understanding of the manner in which the interest rate was fixed was that it was done under a formula whereby the rate should not exceed the interest rate on long term government bonds by more than 2\ per cent. I said that according to my information long term government bonds had slipped and I believed their rate to be under 3 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Four per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister rose and said they were four per cent. I sent for the Financial Post and that is not the position. If I read correctly the government bond investment schedule appearing here it is more like the statement which I put on the record. It may be that there is a particular form of bond that bears interest at the rate of four per cent but I think the house and the minister will agree that the average bond which is bought on the market or which has been held by investors for some time certainly does not give a yield of four per cent which would indicate that if that formula is correct the interest rate should be below six per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The information I have from the officials is that the yield on a 20-year theoretical Canada bond as at the beginning of the month was four per cent and that figure is set by the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand it is not on the 20-year series but on the average purchase of bonds in the investment market.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is described as a 20-year theoretical Canada bond. I know the calculation is made in the Department of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, the reply which I received a few moments ago from
the minister to the effect that only 191 units were approved in New Brunswick during the last month makes it quite obvious, as I said earlier, that the scheme is not altogether practical in New Brunswick or the Atlantic provinces generally. Can the minister tell the committee if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation can supply plans and specifications for low cost units? What I mean by low cost units is the type of units which would meet the needs of fishermen or low income wage earners such as those I mentioned in my remarks earning from $45 to $60 per week. The type of home I have in mind is one which is worth from $5,000 to $6,000.
I understand such plans are available for Newfoundland. If so, would it be possible for fishermen from other Atlantic areas or low income wage earners, to write central mortgage requesting information, plans or specifications of houses? Could they be advised that such plans are available? Am I correct in intimating that such plans are available for houses of this type?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not sure of that. I do
not see any reason why they should not be.
I find I have given the committee wrong information. These repayments have to be made to the receiver general by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to pay off the debentures which are owed to the treasury, so the fund is not a revolving fund after all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask a question of the minister? During the course of the debate I suggested that he might comment on the announcement made by his colleague concerning the construction of housing in Montreal, wherein he stated that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works would both introduce legislation. The Minister of Public Works has introduced his legislation, which I presume his colleague had in mind, but I think the hon. gentleman gave some indication that there would be a reduction in the rate of interest. I quoted from Le Devoir, and I do not want to quote that again, but I notice the minister did not comment on that statement when he spoke.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I know of no such plan. It may be that the newspaper report is incorrect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister if he has any idea as to the number of men who would be employed in the field of housing under this expenditure? For instance, I presume some study must have been made by the government since they have been in office concerning the number of people who would be employed in the construction of homes, having regard to the funds already voted

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: in the month of November last year. Is the minister able to indicate that, and relate it to what is being voted now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Employment would run about four men per unit for a period of six months. In addition to that, of course, there would be people making furniture, fixtures and producing lumber-all the other occupations incidental to housebuilding.

Would the minister have available the figures showing the number of units which have been built under central mortgage plans and which are now unoccupied or for sale? There must be certain sections of the country where there is an excess of housing units, which units are unoccupied and available for sale. Has the minister any figures showing that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, the homes built under the small homes loan plan have been selling very rapidly. I gave figures yesterday for completions to the end of April. The number was 1,722. The hon. member will realize from that figure that a great majority of those homes have not yet been completed. There seems to be a very strong demand for the homes, and this has been the situation all along.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before I ask my question, may I thank the minister for the interest which he has shown in the question of land costs and the manner in which that item has risen. Has he or his officers, since the debate has been in progress, given any consideration to what kind of remedy, investigation or inquiry could be made by the crown corporation to the end of assisting in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The corporation has been following this situation very closely ever since I have been minister, and even before under my predecessor, the Hon. Robert Winters. This is one of our most serious problems, and it is one for which we are not directly responsible-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I realize that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-and which we cannot control; that is the awkward part of it.
National Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Not only Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but also provincial governments, municipal governments and housing authorities all over Canada, are very much concerned about this question. Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday night, before moving the adjournment of the debate, I had the opportunity to tender you my congratulations on your recent appointment. Today, I hasten to state that we are certain that you will fill this post, as you did before, with dignity and competence.
When expressing my feelings of admiration, I am not forgetting the hon. members for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) and Spadina (Mr. Rea) who were recently appointed, respectively, chairman and deputy chairman of the committees of the whole.
Moreover, I congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Lafreniere and Mr. Nielsen), because the two hon. members for Quebec-Montmorency and the Yukon, while residing in entirely opposite areas, have several qualifications in common, like their youth, their dynamism and perspicacity, both of which are necessary to any man engaged in public affairs.
I also take this opportunity today to thank publicly, on behalf of the province of Quebec, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has kindly appointed two other members from our province to his federal cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will bear on three aspects: constitutional, economic and cultural.
In the economic field, it is an undeniable fact that our problems are very numerous. Besides, it is for this reason that, on June 10, 1957 and March 31, 1958, the people of Canada changed teams so that these problems might be solved.
The root of these problems lies in inflation, unemployment and a too great economic dependence upon the United States.
The causes of these problems are both remote and immediate. Among the remote causes, we could mention the political pattern of Canada which is, as it were, a challenge even to geography.
We know that whereas the Canadian territory extends over a thin band from east to west, our economic regions run north and

south. It will be said, that this diversity might be beneficial in due course for the Canadian nation. That is true but, at the present time, it is such as to give rise to varied and aggravated problems because of the dispersion of a small population over a vast territory. The settling of this Canadian territory of ours has cost a great deal, and it is not, as yet, an economic operation.
Among the remote causes of the problems facing this country, we might add the absence of co-operation and of an inefficient co-ordination in economic policy between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. Whereas the present federal government is prepared for deficit financing, because of the present economic needs, the provinces are still aiming at surplus budgeting.
Among the remote causes of the problems facing this country, a great many are related to the Canadian confederation itself, such as, for example, the sharing of powers and the presence of two principal races within our borders.
Mr. Speaker, we might well ask if the Canadian constitution which was written in the year 1867 has not become a strait jacket for the 1958 economy.
Among the immediate causes of our problems, we find unemployment and inflation. I will make no attempt at this time to enumerate every reason for this economic recession, far from it. I will merely list the causes of economic recession which were brought about, undoubtedly, by the last Liberal administration:	credit restrictions,
the maintenance of heavy taxes, a surplus budget when economic needs called for the contrary, mass immigration-in June 1957, one immigrant entered the country every 90 seconds-accumulation of surpluses, too great an economic dependence on our neighbours to the south, the dumping of textile products. And we also have waste in government expenditures.
Our problems in Canada cannot be solved along a straight line but rather as a whole. Indeed, they must not be considered separately, far from it. They must be considered as a whole because they are interrelated, they bear on one another just as the spokes of a wheel bear on the rim and insure its smooth running. When a spoke fails, all the other spokes are weakened in proportion and the rim can break on the run. If one of the spokes is too long, the whole wheel is unbalanced to the point of endangering the driving.
So, the solution to our problems in Canada are well summarized in this principle which our government and our eminent leader, the
The Address*-Mr. Allard right hon. member for Prince Albert, have applied since coming to power on June 10, and which they continue to apply for the prosperity of the Canadian economy. This principle consists in putting and leaving as much money as possible in the hands of the Canadian taxpayer while stepping up large public works.
This wiser economic method is not new. It is as old as the centuries which have put it into use. In fact, in Rome, in the early days of the republic, senators Appius and Flaminius applied that economic method when they constructed the famous Appian and Flaminian ways.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate our government and our right hon. Prime Minister on their planning to apply that most efficient economic doctrine to the solution of our Canadian problems and I would ask them to be kind enough to consider the problem of our municipalities and that of our school boards and to determine whether it would not be possible for them to pay municipal and school taxes on their buildings and even to eliminate the 10 per cent tax on all purchases made by the municipalities and the school boards.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, among Canadian problems there is one which concerns my own beautiful constituency of Sherbrooke, that is the textile problem. The textile industry is rated second among Canadian industries, according to the number of employees engaged in its operation. There are 725 factories in our country located chiefly in Ontario and in Quebec. Whereas 52 per cent of all Canadian manufacturing industries are owned by outsiders, 80 per cent of the textile industry belongs to Canadians. It is, therefore, our own industry, built up with our own funds and through our own initiative.
In the province of Quebec this industry, to be found in 354 establishments, supports 20 important towns and provides work for over
47,000	workers. In Quebec the textile industry is the second largest job provider in the province. In Sherbrooke, there are 14 factories which employ 44.1 per cent of the workers, both male and female. 1 have ascertained that since 1951 the population of Sherbrooke has increased by 17.3 per cent, but that textile employment has declined by 18.2 per cent.
On discovering so much uneasiness and unemployment in our textile industry we must expose the profound and remote causes. Nothing satisfactory was done by the former Liberal administration since 1935, either to adjust the customs tariff or to prohibit the import into Canada of foreign products which

The Address-Mr. Allard flood our markets and paralyse production in our own industry. More especially, during the past 10 years, the former Liberal administration has been giving free rein to foreign competitors and, in a blind and improvident manner, has left our Canadian market at the mercy and whim of imports coming in from Japan, the Indies, Italy, England, West Germany and the United States.
It is very commendable to enter into collaboration, but it should never be done at the risk of sacrificing our economic freedom and becoming a victim and slave to enterprising countries. How can one expect Canadian industries to compete with foreign products when the cost of production is not to be compared? In Canada the average hourly wage is $1.20, whereas Japanese and Hindu labourers work for between 12 and 15 cents an hour. By allowing imports of this kind the Liberal party has for many years openly encouraged what is commonly known as dumping. By "dumping", we mean the great quantity of surplus imported merchandise which is allowed to enter Canada.
During the course of the twenty-third parliament and under the high direction of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) the government ordered that an investigation be made by the federal commission on tariff rates in order to study the whole Canadian textile industry. Since the brilliant victory of March 31 last, the representatives of the Prime Minister in the eastern townships have met at Sherbrooke in order to form a special committee to study economic and industrial problems.
I had the honour to be elected the first president of this special committee. Therefore, in the name of the members of this committee and also in the name of those who are directly or indirectly interested in this highly important industry in our country, I propose to my government the following possible solutions:
1.	A complete revision of our tariff rates, the imposing of which should take into consideration the Canadian consumption.
2.	The possibility of imposing customs duty, per square yard, instead of on weight per pound.
3.	The abolishment of preferential tariff for the Indies.
4.	To step up customs supervision.
5.	To revise, in the law, the definition of the word "dumping" so that the price of the imported product will include the total cost of production, plus a reasonable margin, covering selling and administration costs, and profit.
6.	To form, in the heart of this federal commission on tariff rates, a permanent committee to study the problems of the textile industry.

7.	To ascertain that the textile products launched on the Canadian market be labelled in such a way as to indicate clearly both the quality and the place of origin.
8.	To request that an economic survey be made of the nature of our exports and imports, in order to arrive at a better balance of our commercial exchanges with other countries.
9.	To suggest that an economic orientation council be formed, in the heart of the United Nations, or a like organization, to co-ordinate production between the interested parties.
10.	To form, if possible, a special committee in the House of Commons to study this problem which is both urgent and national.
Such are the conclusions I submit most respectfully.

Mr. Speaker, on the constitutional level we should say that this is a matter which is at the source of all our Canadian problems. We must indeed govern under the constitution in this country, and comply with the legislation we pass in this house, and doing so, we must keep in mind the spirit which moved the fathers of confederation.
As I said a few moments ago, because of economic conditions, and following the economic ups and downs which have marked the years since 1867, we may wonder whether it would not be wise to amend the Canadian constitution in some economic areas. Well, as long as this constitution of 1867 is not amended with the assent of all and every party concerned, we must, in opposition to the Liberals who undermined and sometimes ignored it, respect our Canadian constitution. I sincerely believe that the Conservative party, which presided over the birth of confederation, is the one which will restore in our country the confederative spirit. And it is precisely the feeling which the present Prime Minister expressed, on November 19 last, in this very House of Commons, when he said: "Ottawa has ceased to dictate its will to the provinces."
In 1867, the two principal races and the four provinces of the time met together in order to establish a central government and entrust to it certain tasks, fields of action and problems which were then common to those provinces, such as money, mail and external affairs. The provinces reserved for themselves particular fields of action and privileges which are outlined under section 92 of the British North America Act.

In so doing, the Canadian provinces, and all those which joined them later in that confederative spirit, founded what we call Canadian federalism. Canadian federalism is essentially a system of autonomous governments, that is to say governments, federal as well as provincial, which are absolute masters in their respective and exclusive fields, and those governments must co-operate in fields of common interest, such as agriculture and immigration, as prescribed by section 95 of the British North America Act.
Those are the principles which the courts have confirmed several times. Let me recall the judgments of the Privy Council to this effect, particularly in the aeronautic case, the Great West Saddlery case and Edwards case, in which it was laid down as a principle that a great majority of the Canadian people can not live by state subsidies, that, in peacetime, the national interest can in no way justify the intervention of the central power, that the provincial governments are autonomous and absolute masters in their exclusive fields, and that no government has the right to do indirectly what it is prevented by law to do directly.
Well, Mr. Speaker, when the Canadian provinces formed the Canadian federation in 1867, they did so not with the intention of renouncing their own subsistence and vitality, far from it, but rather to ensure their own vitality and we can find an indication of this in the preamble to the British North America Act, from which I quote the following:
And whereas such a Union would contribute to the Welfare of the Provinces . . .
Well, Mr. Speaker, is it not logical to believe that national prosperity cannot exist without the prosperity of the provinces and municipalities which compose the Canadian nation? In order to recreate that Canadian reality, that constitutional reality, should the government not consider handing back, in a certain proportion and gradually, the direct taxes which belong to the provinces in accordance with paragraph 2 of section 92? Thus the provinces would have the financial means of fulfilling their own obligations, the federal government would be in a better position to enhance and improve its own fields of action, members of Parliament could study further the complex problems of international politics, which raise in the souls and hearts of all those who keep abreast of them a deep concern, as the world goes through-as we all know and feel-a very critical phase in international affairs.
The Address-Mr. Allard
In the cultural area we must endeavour to foster what I would call national understanding. Our fine country would grow in the social and economic fields if all Canadians shared the same feelings and sought the same objectives.
I am sorry to have to say so today, but during the last election campaign in the province of Quebec I saw the Liberal party attempt to appeal to racial, language and religious prejudices. This party, which was so strong an advocate of national unity, was the very one who attempted by all kinds of insidious means to pit Canadians one against the other. We must deeply regret such antinational and antidemocratic attempts.
Mr. Speaker, in the 23rd parliament, as well as in the recent election campaign and again last Tuesday night, I heard the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) insinuate that the province of Quebec was divided against itself. Well, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Laurier used the word division, my eyes automatically turned to the other side of the house and, to the exclusion of that part of the gallant Progressive Conservative team, I see before me, on the other side of the house, that they are not only divided but diminished, contracted and almost eliminated.
The hon. member for Laurier, who has been living in the province of Quebec for a few years only, seeks to represent the aspirations of that province but he should not forget that Quebec has an amazing memory, that it is a province which remembers.
We remember, Mr. Speaker, that the present member for Laurier when he represented a constituency from another province and was a member of a federal Liberal government was the one who fought for many years against the construction of a railway line in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out in the last part of my speech, we should try to establish in this country real national understanding. In 1867, Canadians wanted

to create a national entity. They did want to create this entity by stressing the equality between all citizens. In 1867, the prime minister of the Canadian confederation, the Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald stated that, in this country, there were no more victors nor vanquished, no majority nor minority, but that all citizens were equal. During the recent election campaign, the present Prime Minister expressed the same feelings, i.e. not the policy of a group or of a province, but a national policy, a democratic and Canadian policy. The Prime Minister advocated that same principle in Halifax, Vancouver, Montreal, Sherbrooke and in all Canadian provinces. And that is why we now see, in our great land of Canada, different mentalities, different races, religions and, as a result, different economic attitudes.
Canadians must attempt to find a common denominator and in so doing they will manage to find formulas that make for balance between each group and each area.
For a number of years the Liberal party preached national unity. If we are to give its proper meaning to the word unity, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that that word cannot be applied to the peculiar characteristics of our country. We know that unity means loss of identity and assimilation. In this country every group, every race, while wishing to live within a magnificent and rich Canadian mosaic, also wishes to conserve its respective characteristics and traditions.
This is the way in which I look at national understanding. What I mean is that Canadians of different races, different religions, different traditions, should wish to live together and tolerate each other good humouredly. That is what I call national understanding. After we have reached, in the very near future I hope, a higher degree of national understanding, it will become easy for our government to adopt officially a distinctive national flag as well as a national anthem.
In order to favour the quick blossoming of this national understanding, our government should entrust the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or any other appropriate department with the following functions:
1.	To favour contacts between Canadians of various areas;
2.	To set up a publicity campaign so that Canadians may know one another better;
3.	To inaugurate low cost interprovincial travel at specified periods of the year;

4.	To encourage an increased exchange of university students between various provinces during the summer months;
5.	To invite federal members of parliament to give lectures in various provinces.

There is no one in a better position to appreciate that than the Liberals who were in power until 1957. Indeed, the Liberal government in the last 22 years it was in power had managed to improve the lot of the farmer in a sure and constant way by the passage of legislation which has never been proved valueless. It is over this period that we have seen an increase in the sale of agricultural products which in 1936 were estimated at $536,000,000 as against $2,600,000,000 in 1955.
